# Overview



Welcome to the LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator) documentation. This page provides a high-level introduction to LAMMPS, its purpose, and the structure of the codebase, designed specifically for developers new to the project.

Sources: [README](README#L1-L18), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L1-L15)

## What is LAMMPS?

LAMMPS is a classical molecular dynamics simulation code designed to run efficiently on parallel computers. Developed at Sandia National Laboratories with funding from the U.S. Department of Energy, it is an open-source code distributed under the GNU General Public License (GPL) version 2. LAMMPS provides a powerful platform for simulating atomic, molecular, and coarse-grained systems across a wide range of scientific applications including materials science, chemistry, physics, and engineering.

The software excels at large-scale simulations, capable of handling systems from a few atoms to millions, making it ideal for researchers investigating complex phenomena at the atomic scale. Its modular architecture allows users to extend functionality through packages, and it supports multiple parallel computing paradigms including MPI, OpenMP, and GPU acceleration.

Sources: [README](README#L1-L18), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L1-L15)

## Repository Architecture

The LAMMPS repository is organized into logical directories that serve distinct purposes in the development workflow. Understanding this structure is essential for navigating the codebase effectively.

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[LAMMPS Repository] --> B[Source Code]
    A --> C[Documentation]
    A --> D[Examples & Tests]
    A --> E[Build System]
    A --> F[Supporting Resources]
    
    B --> B1[src/ - Core C++ source files]
    B --> B2[fortran/ - Fortran 2003 module]
    B --> B3[python/ - Python integration]
    
    C --> C1[doc/ - Manual and documentation]
    
    D --> D1[examples/ - Example problems]
    D --> D2[bench/ - Benchmark tests]
    D --> D3[unittest/ - Unit tests]
    
    E --> E1[cmake/ - CMake build files]
    
    F --> F1[potentials/ - Interatomic potential files]
    F --> F2[tools/ - Pre/post-processing tools]
    F --> F3[third_party/ - External libraries]
```

Sources: [README](README#L19-L35), [Get repo structure: top level](.)

## Directory Structure Overview

### Core Components

The **src/** directory contains the core C++ source code that implements LAMMPS functionality. This is where the simulation engine, particle interaction calculations, and fundamental algorithms reside. The code is organized into classes that handle different aspects of molecular dynamics simulations.

The **doc/** directory houses the comprehensive LAMMPS documentation, including the manual, tutorials, and reference materials. Documentation can be generated locally in HTML or PDF formats.

Sources: [README](README#L19-L35), [doc/README](doc/README#L1-L10)

### Build and Development

The **cmake/** directory contains CMake build files for modern cross-platform compilation. CMake is the recommended build system for LAMMPS, providing flexibility and ease of configuration.

The **unittest/** directory contains test programs used with CTest for automated testing, ensuring code stability across different platforms and configurations.

Sources: [README](README#L19-L25), [bench/README](bench/README#L1-L10)

### Examples and Benchmarks

The **examples/** directory is a valuable learning resource containing three categories of sample problems:

| Category | Description | Purpose |
|----------|-------------|---------|
| Lowercase directories | Simple test problems (e.g., `melting`, `crack`) | Quick demonstrations of LAMMPS features |
| Uppercase directories | Complex multi-file examples | Real-world simulation scenarios |
| PACKAGES subdirectory | Style-specific package tests | Validation of individual package functionality |

The **bench/** directory contains standardized benchmark problems used to evaluate LAMMPS performance across different hardware configurations and parallel implementations. These benchmarks are essential for performance optimization and scaling studies.

Sources: [examples/README](examples/README#L1-L50), [bench/README](bench/README#L1-L25)

### Supporting Resources

The **potentials/** directory provides a comprehensive collection of interatomic potential files including EAM, MEAM, SNAP, ReaxFF, and many other potentials. These files are ready-to-use resources for various materials systems.

The **tools/** directory contains utilities for pre-processing (creating input files) and post-processing (analyzing output data), including conversion scripts, visualization helpers, and analysis tools.

The **python/** directory contains the LAMMPS Python module that enables Python scripting workflows and integration with scientific Python ecosystems like NumPy and Jupyter.

Sources: [README](README#L26-L35), [tools/README](tools/README#L1-L25), [python/README](python/README#L1-L10), [potentials/](potentials/)

> [!TIP]
> The `potentials/` directory contains hundreds of potential files covering elements from Al to Zn and various compound systems. These are production-ready files that can be used directly in simulations without modification.

## Key Features and Capabilities

LAMMPS provides an extensive set of features that make it suitable for diverse simulation scenarios:

### Simulation Models

| Feature Category | Examples |
|-----------------|----------|
| **Pair Potentials** | Lennard-Jones, EAM, MEAM, ReaxFF, Tersoff, SNAP |
| **Bonded Interactions** | Bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers, CHARMM force fields |
| **Long-Range Electrostatics** | PPPM, Ewald, Reaction Field |
| **Advanced Methods** | NEB, free energy calculations, replica exchange, MC/MD hybrid |

### Parallel Computing

LAMMPS supports multiple parallel computing strategies to maximize performance on modern hardware architectures:

- **MPI parallelization** for distributed memory systems
- **OpenMP threading** for shared memory parallelism
- **GPU acceleration** through CUDA, HIP, and OpenCL backends
- **Kokkos performance portability** for portable code across different architectures

These parallel capabilities allow LAMMPS to scale efficiently from laptops to supercomputers with millions of processors.

Sources: [README](README#L10-L18), [examples/README](examples/README#L80-L120)

## Getting Started with LAMMPS

### Quick Access Paths

![LAMMPS Repository](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/README?raw=true)

The repository provides clear entry points for different needs:

- **Learn LAMMPS**: Start with examples in the `examples/` directory
- **Performance Testing**: Use benchmarks in `bench/` to evaluate your system
- **Development Work**: Explore `src/` and contribute through the standard workflow
- **Integration**: Leverage `python/` module for scientific computing workflows

### Example Workflow

A typical workflow for learning LAMMPS involves:

1. **Exploring Examples**: Browse simple examples like `melting` or `crack` to understand input script structure
2. **Running Benchmarks**: Execute benchmark problems to verify installation and assess performance
3. **Modifying Scripts**: Adapt examples to your specific research needs
4. **Consulting Documentation**: Refer to the manual for detailed command syntax and physics explanations

Sources: [examples/README](examples/README#L120-L140), [bench/README](bench/README#L70-L100)

## Community and Support

LAMMPS is maintained by an active development team and benefits from contributions from researchers worldwide. The official website (www.lammps.org) provides extensive documentation, tutorials, and community forums.

For developers interested in contributing, the project follows established GitHub workflow practices with clear guidelines for code submissions and testing procedures.

Sources: [README](README#L28-L32), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L1-L20)

# Quick Start



This page guides you through your first steps with LAMMPS (Large-scale Atomic/Molecular Massively Parallel Simulator), a classical molecular dynamics code designed for efficient parallel computing. You'll learn how to obtain LAMMPS, run your first simulation, and explore available resources—all within minutes of getting started.

Sources: [README](README#L1-L20), [CITATION.cff](CITATION.cff#L1-L15)

## Getting LAMMPS

LAMMPS is distributed as an open-source package under the GNU GPL version 2. You can obtain it through multiple methods:

![LAMMPS GitHub Repository](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/README?raw=true)

| **Method** | **Command** | **Best For** |
|------------|-------------|--------------|
| Git Clone | `git clone https://github.com/lammps/lammps.git` | Latest development version, contributors |
| Download Tarball | From www.lammps.org | Stable releases, production use |
| Package Manager | System-specific packages | Quick installation, managed updates |

The repository structure includes essential directories: `src/` (source files), `examples/` (sample problems), `cmake/` (build system), `doc/` (documentation), and `tools/` (pre/post-processing utilities).

Sources: [README](README#L20-L40)

## Architecture Overview

LAMMPS follows a modular architecture that separates simulation logic from computational implementations:

```mermaid
graph TB
    A[LAMMPS User] --> B[Input Scripts]
    B --> C[LAMMPS Core Engine]
    C --> D[Atom Classes]
    C --> E[Force Fields]
    C --> F[Integrators]
    C --> G[Output/Analysis]
    D --> H[Atom Styles]
    E --> I[Pair/Bond/Angle/Dihedral]
    F --> J[Fix Commands]
    G --> K[Dump/Thermo/Compute]
    C --> L[Parallel Execution]
    L --> M[MPI]
    L --> N[OpenMP]
    L --> O[GPU/Kokkos]
```

This architecture enables flexible simulation setup through input scripts while maintaining computational efficiency through parallel execution strategies. The core processes commands sequentially but distributes computational work across available processors.

Sources: [README](README#L1-L15), [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L30)

## Running Your First Simulation

The quickest way to verify your installation is running a simple molecular dynamics simulation. Navigate to the `examples/melt/` directory which contains a 3D Lennard-Jones melt example:

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1-L10)

```bash
cd examples/melt
lmp -in in.melt
```

This simulation demonstrates core LAMMPS concepts:

| **Section** | **Purpose** | **Key Commands** |
|-------------|-------------|------------------|
| Units & Style | Define simulation units and atom representation | `units lj`, `atom_style atomic` |
| System Setup | Create simulation box and atoms | `lattice`, `region`, `create_box`, `create_atoms` |
| Interactions | Define particle interactions | `pair_style lj/cut 2.5`, `pair_coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0 2.5` |
| Integration | Control time evolution | `fix 1 all nve` |
| Output | Monitor simulation progress | `thermo 50`, `run 250` |

The output log file shows simulation details including number of atoms created (4000 atoms in a 10×10×10 fcc lattice), computational parameters, and timing information.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1-L34), [examples/melt/log.8Apr21.melt.g++.1](examples/melt/log.8Apr21.melt.g++.1#L1-L35)

## Understanding Example Categories

LAMMPS provides a rich collection of examples organized by complexity:

![Examples Directory Structure](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/examples/README?raw=true)

| **Category** | **Naming Convention** | **Description** | **Run Time** |
|--------------|---------------------|-----------------|--------------|
| Simple Tests | Lowercase (e.g., `melt`, `min`) | Quick verification of basic functionality | Seconds to minutes |
| Complex Problems | Uppercase (e.g., `ASPHERE`, `HEAT`) | Advanced techniques and specific applications | Minutes to hours |
| Package Tests | `PACKAGES/` subdirectories | Specialized features from optional packages | Varies by package |

The `examples/README` explains that each problem includes input scripts (`in.*`), sample log files, and optional visualization outputs. Most simple examples are 2D models designed for rapid execution.

Sources: [examples/README](examples/README#L1-L25), [get_repo_structure/examples](#L3-L85)

## Build Configuration Presets

The CMake build system includes pre-configured presets for different use cases. The `basic.cmake` preset activates commonly-used packages:

```cmake
set(ALL_PACKAGES KSPACE MANYBODY MOLECULE RIGID)
foreach(PKG ${ALL_PACKAGES})
  set(PKG_${PKG} ON CACHE BOOL "" FORCE)
endforeach()
```

Available presets include:
- **basic.cmake**: Core packages for common inputs
- **all_on.cmake**: Enable all packages
- **kokkos-*.cmake**: Performance portability across CPUs/GPUs
- **gpu-cuda.cmake**: NVIDIA GPU acceleration
- **windows.cmake**: Windows-specific configurations

Sources: [cmake/presets/basic.cmake](cmake/presets/basic.cmake#L1-L9), [get_repo_structure/cmake](#L5-L33)

## Python Integration Quick Start

LAMMPS provides a Python module enabling programmatic simulation control. The `python/examples/simple.py` demonstrates basic usage:

```bash
cd python/examples
python simple.py
```

Python integration allows you to:
- Drive LAMMPS simulations from Python scripts
- Extract and analyze simulation data with NumPy
- Combine LAMMPS with scientific Python ecosystems
- Use Jupyter notebooks for interactive workflows

The `examples/python/` directory contains input scripts like `in.python` that show how to embed Python functions within LAMMPS input files using the `python` command.

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py), [examples/python/in.python](examples/python/in.python#L1-L40), [get_repo_structure/python](#L5-L27)

## Verification and Testing

After building LAMMPS, verify your installation using available testing resources:

| **Resource** | **Purpose** | **Location** |
|--------------|-------------|--------------|
| Simple Examples | Verify basic functionality | `examples/melt/`, `examples/min/` |
| Benchmarks | Test performance and scalability | `bench/` directory |
| Unit Tests | Validate specific components | `unittest/` directory |
| Regression Tests | Check for code changes impact | `tools/regression-tests/` |

The `bench/README` describes standardized benchmarks with 32,000 atoms running for 100 timesteps, suitable for both serial and parallel performance evaluation.

Sources: [bench/README](bench/README#L1-L30), [get_repo_structure/bench](#L5-L75)

## Visualization Tools

LAMMPS supports multiple visualization output formats in example scripts:

- **Dump files**: Text format compatible with Ovito, VMD, AtomEye
- **Image output**: JPG snapshots (requires JPG library)
- **Movie output**: MPG videos (requires FFMPEG library)

Uncomment the appropriate `dump` commands in example input scripts to generate visualization files. The `tools/` directory contains various pre/post-processing utilities including `tools/python/` for data analysis and conversion.

Sources: [examples/README](examples/README#L35-L55), [get_repo_structure/tools](#L5-L242)

## Common First Commands

When starting with LAMMPS, these input script commands appear most frequently:

| **Command Category** | **Typical Commands** | **First Simulation Usage** |
|---------------------|---------------------|--------------------------|
| Setup | `units`, `atom_style`, `dimension` | Define simulation framework |
| Geometry | `lattice`, `region`, `create_box`, `create_atoms` | Build atomic structure |
| Properties | `mass`, `velocity` | Set physical properties |
| Interactions | `pair_style`, `pair_coeff`, `bond_style` | Define force fields |
| Integration | `fix`, `run`, `minimize` | Control dynamics |
| Output | `thermo`, `dump` | Monitor results |

The `examples/min/in.min` example shows how to combine dynamics (`run 1000`) with energy minimization (`minimize`) in a single script.

Sources: [examples/min/in.min](examples/min/in.min#L1-L45)

## Next Steps

After completing this Quick Start guide, continue your LAMMPS journey with these resources:

- [Installation and Build System](3-installation-and-build-system) - Detailed compilation instructions and package configuration

For immediate exploration, browse the `examples/` directory categories or examine input scripts matching your research domain. The comprehensive documentation is available online at https://docs.lammps.org/Manual.html.


# Installation and Build System



This guide covers installing and building LAMMPS using the modern CMake-based build system. LAMMPS offers flexibility through multiple build configurations, package selections, and platform-specific optimizations tailored for different use cases from basic simulations to high-performance computing environments.

## Build System Architecture

LAMMPS utilizes a modular CMake build system that separates concerns between core compilation, optional packages, external libraries, and platform-specific configurations. The build process follows a hierarchical structure where components are conditionally compiled based on user requirements and system capabilities.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[LAMMPS Build System] --> B[CMake Configuration]
    B --> C[Core Library<br/>lammps]
    B --> D[Optional Packages<br/>80+ packages]
    B --> E[External Libraries<br/>kokkos, gpu, lepton, etc.]
    B --> F[Build Tools<br/>lammps-gui, tools]
    
    D --> G[Compute Styles]
    D --> H[Pair Potentials]
    D --> I[Fix Commands]
    D --> J[Utilities]
    
    E --> K[Kokkos Portability]
    E --> L[GPU Acceleration]
    E --> M[FFTW/MKL]
    
    C --> N[Executable: lmp]
    F --> O[lammps-gui]
    
    style A fill:#e1f5fe
    style C fill:#c8e6c9
    style N fill:#fff9c4
    style O fill:#fff9c4
```

The repository structure organizes these components logically:

![Repository Structure Overview](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/cmake/CMakeLists.txt?raw=true)

| Directory | Purpose | Key Contents |
|-----------|---------|--------------|
| `cmake/` | CMake build system | Main CMakeLists.txt, Modules, presets |
| `src/` | Core source code | LAMMPS kernel, style implementations |
| `lib/` | External libraries | kokkos, gpu, lepton, molfile, etc. |
| `tools/` | Pre/post-processing | Utilities for data conversion, analysis |
| `doc/` | Documentation | Sphinx source, build scripts |
| `examples/` | Example inputs | Simulation templates by topic |

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L80), [README](README#L1-L60)

## Prerequisites

Before building LAMMPS, ensure your system meets these requirements:

### Core Requirements
- **C++ Compiler**: GCC 9.3+, Clang 10.0+, Intel 19.0+, or MSVC 2019+ with C++17 support
- **CMake**: Version 3.20 or later
- **MPI**: For parallel builds (optional but recommended)
- **Python**: 3.8+ (optional, for Python module)

### Platform-Specific Notes
- **Linux**: GCC or Clang recommended; Intel compilers supported via presets
- **macOS**: AppleClang 10.0+ or GCC via Homebrew; Xcode command-line tools required
- **Windows**: MSVC 2019+ or MinGW; Visual Studio recommended

> [!TIP]
> CMake 3.20 is strictly required. Older versions will fail with policy errors. Check with `cmake --version` before proceeding.

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L1-L15), [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L128-L160)

## Basic CMake Build

The simplest build uses CMake's out-of-source build pattern with minimal configuration:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Clone LAMMPS] --> B[Create build directory]
    B --> C[Run cmake configuration]
    C --> D[Build with make/ninja]
    D --> E[Install or test]
    
    style C fill:#ffe0b2
    style D fill:#c8e6c9
```

**Step-by-step process:**

```bash
# 1. Navigate to LAMMPS directory
cd lammps/

# 2. Create and enter build directory
mkdir build && cd build

# 3. Configure with default settings
cmake ../cmake

# 4. Build LAMMPS (adjust -j for available cores)
cmake --build . -j 8

# 5. Install to default location (~/.local on Linux/macOS)
cmake --install .
```

**Key configuration options:**

| Option | Default | Description |
|--------|---------|-------------|
| `-C <preset>` | none | Load configuration preset (see below) |
| `-DPKG_<PACKAGE>=ON` | OFF | Enable specific package |
| `-DBUILD_SHARED_LIBS=ON` | OFF | Build shared library instead of static |
| `-DCMAKE_INSTALL_PREFIX` | `~/.local` | Installation directory |
| `-DBUILD_MPI=ON` | auto-detected | Enable MPI support |

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L50-L70), [README](README#L35-L60)

## Build Presets

LAMMPS provides pre-configured CMake presets in `cmake/presets/` for common scenarios. These simplify configuration by bundling package selections and compiler settings.

### Available Presets

| Preset | Description | Use Case |
|--------|-------------|----------|
| `basic.cmake` | Minimal packages (KSPACE, MANYBODY, MOLECULE, RIGID) | Quick builds, simple systems |
| `most.cmake` | Wide range of packages, requires some external libs | General-purpose simulations |
| `all_on.cmake` | All packages enabled | Maximum features, longest build time |
| `kokkos-cuda.cmake` | Kokkos with CUDA GPU support | NVIDIA GPU acceleration |
| `intel.cmake` | Intel compilers with optimizations | Intel CPUs, AVX-512 |
| `windows.cmake` | Windows-compatible packages | MSVC/MinGW builds |

**Using presets:**

```bash
# Basic build with common packages
cmake -C ../cmake/presets/basic.cmake ../cmake

# Kokkos GPU build
cmake -C ../cmake/presets/kokkos-cuda.cmake ../cmake

# Intel compiler optimization
cmake -C ../cmake/presets/intel.cmake ../cmake

# Windows with Visual Studio
cmake -C ../cmake/presets/windows.cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" ../cmake
```

Sources: [cmake/presets/basic.cmake](cmake/presets/basic.cmake#L1-L9), [cmake/presets/most.cmake](cmake/presets/most.cmake#L1-L78), [cmake/presets/all_on.cmake](cmake/presets/all_on.cmake#L1-L102), [cmake/presets/kokkos-cuda.cmake](cmake/presets/kokkos-cuda.cmake#L1-L14), [cmake/presets/intel.cmake](cmake/presets/intel.cmake#L1-L29), [cmake/presets/windows.cmake](cmake/presets/windows.cmake#L1-L76)

## Package Selection

LAMMPS functionality is modularized through packages. Each package adds specific features like potential styles, compute commands, or fix operations.

### Enabling Packages

**Individual package selection:**

```bash
cmake -DPKG_KSPACE=ON \
      -DPKG_MANYBODY=ON \
      -DPKG_MOLECULE=ON \
      -DPKG_RIGID=ON \
      ../cmake
```

**Package categories:**

| Category | Example Packages | Functionality |
|----------|------------------|---------------|
| **Physics** | MANYBODY, KSPACE, MOLECULE | EAM potentials, long-range electrostatics, molecular systems |
| **Materials** | GRANULAR, PERI, SPH | Granular flow, peridynamics, smoothed-particle hydrodynamics |
| **ML/AI** | ML-SNAP, ML-IAP, ML-PACE | Machine learning potentials |
| **Accelerators** | GPU, KOKKOS, INTEL | GPU and many-core optimizations |
| **Analysis** | COLVARS, PHONON, REPLICA | Enhanced analysis capabilities |

### Package Dependencies

Some packages require others or external libraries:

```
ML-IAP → ML-SNAP
DIELECTRIC → KSPACE + EXTRA-PAIR
CG-DNA → MOLECULE + ASPHERE
AMOEBA → KSPACE
```

> [!TIP]
> Use `-C ../cmake/presets/all_off.cmake` to reset all packages before enabling specific ones.

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L415-L435), [cmake/presets/all_off.cmake](cmake/presets/all_off.cmake#L1-L100)

## External Libraries

Several packages require external libraries located in `lib/`. CMake handles building these automatically when packages are enabled.

### Automated Library Building

```bash
# Enable packages with external dependencies
cmake -DPKG_KOKKOS=ON \
      -DPKG_GPU=ON \
      -DPKG_ML-SNAP=ON \
      -DPKG_VORONOI=ON \
      ../cmake

# CMake will automatically:
# 1. Download/build Kokkos (if not found)
# 2. Build GPU library
# 3. Download/build ScaFaCoS (for long-range)
# 4. Find/build Voro++ (for Voronoi analysis)
```

### Key External Libraries

| Library | Required By | Description |
|---------|-------------|-------------|
| Kokkos | KOKKOS, ML-* packages | Performance portability layer |
| GPU | GPU package | CUDA/OpenCL acceleration |
| FFTW/MKL | KSPACE, COLVARS | Fast Fourier transforms |
| Voro++ | VORONOI package | Voronoi tessellation |
| NetCDF | NETCDF package | Trajectory I/O |
| ScaFaCoS | SCAFACOS package | Long-range solvers |

Sources: [lib/README](lib/README#L1-L30)

## Platform-Specific Builds

### Linux with GCC/Clang

```bash
# Standard GCC build
cmake -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=g++ \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=gcc \
      -C ../cmake/presets/most.cmake \
      ../cmake

# Clang build with LTO
cmake -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ \
      -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang \
      -DCMAKE_INTERPROCEDURAL_OPTIMIZATION=ON \
      -C ../cmake/presets/most.cmake \
      ../cmake
```

### macOS

```bash
# AppleClang with Homebrew dependencies
cmake -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++ \
      -DPKG_KSPACE=ON \
      -DPKG_MANYBODY=ON \
      -DPKG_MOLECULE=ON \
      -DBUILD_MPI=OFF \
      ../cmake

# Multi-architecture build (ARM64 + x86_64)
cmake -C ../cmake/presets/macos-multiarch.cmake ../cmake
```

### Windows with Visual Studio

```bash
# From Visual Studio Developer Command Prompt
cmake -G "Visual Studio 17 2022" -A x64 ^
      -C ..\cmake\presets\windows.cmake ^
      ..\cmake

cmake --build . --config Release

cmake --install . --config Release
```

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L100-L160), [cmake/presets/macos-multiarch.cmake](cmake/presets/macos-multiarch.cmake#L1-L20)

## Build Tools and Utilities

LAMMPS includes additional tools that can be built alongside the main executable.

### LAMMPS GUI

```bash
# Enable GUI build
cmake -DPKG_MOLFILE=ON \
      -DBUILD_TOOLS=ON \
      ../cmake

cmake --build . --target lammps-gui
```

### Pre/Post-Processing Tools

The `tools/` directory contains standalone utilities for data preparation and analysis:

![LAMMPS Tools](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/tools/README?raw=true)

| Tool | Purpose | Build Method |
|------|---------|--------------|
| `binary2txt` | Convert binary dump to text | `make binary2txt` in tools/ |
| `lmp2cfg` | Convert to AtomEye format | `make lmp2cfg` in tools/ |
| `createatoms` | Generate atom lattices | See tools/createatoms/README |
| `phonon` | Post-process phonon data | CMake in tools/phonon/ |
| `python/*` | Python analysis scripts | No build required |

Sources: [tools/README](tools/README#L1-L63), [tools/Makefile](tools/Makefile#L1-L38)

## Documentation Build

Build the LAMMPS manual locally for offline reference:

```bash
cd doc

# HTML version (requires Python 3.8+, Sphinx, Doxygen)
make html

# PDF version (requires LaTeX with additional packages)
make pdf

# Output locations:
# HTML: doc/html/Manual.html
# PDF:  doc/Manual.pdf
```

### Documentation Requirements

**HTML build:**
- Python 3.8+
- Sphinx
- Doxygen 1.8.10+
- Internet connection (for initial downloads)

**PDF build (additional):**
- LaTeX (TeX Live or MiKTeX)
- Required packages: amsmath, babel, hyperref, geometry, fncychap, and 15+ others

Sources: [doc/README](doc/README#L1-L86)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

### CMake Configuration Failures

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| "CMake 3.20 or higher required" | Update CMake: `pip install cmake --upgrade` or use package manager |
| "Could not find MPI" | Install OpenMPI or MPICH, or set `-DBUILD_MPI=OFF` |
| "C++17 support required" | Ensure compiler supports C++17 (GCC 9.3+, Clang 10+) |
| "omp.h not found" | Install OpenMP headers or set `-DBUILD_OMP=OFF` |

### Build Failures

| Issue | Solution |
|-------|----------|
| "undefined reference to omp" | Link OpenMP: `-DBUILD_OMP=ON` |
| Kokkos build errors | Use system Kokkos: `-DKokkos_DIR=/path/to/kokkos` |
| Out of memory during link | Reduce parallel jobs: `cmake --build . -j 4` |

Sources: [cmake/CMakeLists.txt](cmake/CMakeLists.txt#L440-L500)

```bash
# Check executable
./lmp -h

# Run simple benchmark
cd ../bench
../../build/lmp -in in.lj

# Run regression tests (requires CTEST)
cd ../tools/regression-tests
python run_tests.py
```

# Running Your First Simulation



This page guides you through executing your first molecular dynamics simulation with LAMMPS. You'll learn the fundamental structure of LAMMPS input scripts, understand how to run simulations via command line and Python interfaces, and interpret the output results. This foundation will prepare you for exploring more advanced simulation concepts and techniques.

## Understanding the LAMMPS Simulation Architecture

Before diving into execution, it's essential to understand how LAMMPS organizes simulation workflows. LAMMPS operates through input scripts that define every aspect of your simulation, from units and boundary conditions to interatomic potentials and output specifications. The execution follows a sequential command processing model where each line modifies the simulation state. This modular approach allows you to build complex simulations from simple, well-defined components.

![LAMMPS Examples Directory](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/examples/README?raw=true)

The simulation lifecycle can be visualized as a structured flow from initialization through production and analysis:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A["[Initialize Simulation]"] --> B["[Define Simulation Box]"]
    B --> C["[Create Atoms]"]
    C --> D["[Set Initial Conditions]"]
    D --> E["[Define Potentials]"]
    E --> F["[Specify Fixes]"]
    F --> G["[Configure Output]"]
    G --> H["[Run Simulation]"]
    H --> I["[Analyze Results]"]
    
    A --> A1["[units command]"]
    A --> A2["[atom_style command]"]
    
    B --> B1["[region command]"]
    B --> B2["[create_box command]"]
    
    C --> C1["[lattice command]"]
    C --> C2["[create_atoms command]"]
    
    D --> D1["[velocity command]"]
    D --> D2["[mass command]"]
    
    E --> E1["[pair_style command]"]
    E --> E2["[pair_coeff command]"]
    
    F --> F1["[fix commands]"]
    F --> F2["[neighbor settings]"]
    
    G --> G1["[thermo command]"]
    G --> G2["[dump commands]"]
    
    H --> H1["[run command]"]
    H --> H2["[minimize command]"]
```

Sources: [examples/README](examples/README#L1-L50), [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1-L34)

## Your First Simulation: The Lennard-Jones Melt

We'll start with the classic Lennard-Jones melt example, located in the `examples/melt` directory. This simulation models a simple fluid of particles interacting through the Lennard-Jones potential, making it an ideal starting point for understanding LAMMPS fundamentals. The example demonstrates all essential components of a working simulation while remaining computationally lightweight.

![Lennard-Jones Melt Example](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/examples/melt/in.melt?raw=true)

Let's examine the complete input script and understand each component:

```
# 3d Lennard-Jones melt

units           lj
atom_style      atomic

lattice         fcc 0.8442
region          box block 0 10 0 10 0 10
create_box      1 box
create_atoms    1 box
mass            1 1.0

velocity        all create 3.0 87287 loop geom

pair_style      lj/cut 2.5
pair_coeff      1 1 1.0 1.0 2.5

neighbor        0.3 bin
neigh_modify    every 20 delay 0 check no

fix             1 all nve

#dump           id all atom 50 dump.melt

thermo          50
run             250
```

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1-L34)

### Simulation Initialization

The first two commands establish the fundamental units and atom representation. The `units lj` command selects Lennard-Jones reduced units, where mass, distance, energy, and time are expressed in dimensionless form. The `atom_style atomic` command specifies that atoms are represented simply by their position and type, without additional properties like molecular bonds or charges. These choices significantly simplify the simulation while maintaining physical realism for studying basic liquid behavior.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L2-L3)

### System Geometry and Atom Creation

The simulation box construction begins with defining a face-centered cubic lattice. The `lattice fcc 0.8442` command creates a lattice structure with a density parameter of 0.8442, which corresponds to a reduced density of approximately 0.8442 atoms per unit volume. This particular density is chosen because it represents a liquid state at the target temperature. The lattice command actually doesn't create atoms immediately—it defines the reference structure.

The `region box block 0 10 0 10 0 10` command defines a rectangular simulation domain extending from 0 to 10 in each dimension. The `create_box 1 box` command initializes the simulation box for one atom type, followed by `create_atoms 1 box` which actually places atoms at all lattice sites within the defined region. This approach creates a perfectly ordered initial configuration of 4000 atoms (10×10×10 unit cells, with 4 atoms per fcc unit cell).

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L5-L7)

### Initial Conditions and Mass Assignment

Setting atom masses is straightforward: `mass 1 1.0` assigns a mass of 1.0 (in reduced units) to atom type 1. The velocity initialization uses `velocity all create 3.0 87287 loop geom`, which generates random velocities for all atoms corresponding to a temperature of 3.0 reduced units. The seed value 87287 ensures reproducibility while the `loop geom` option distributes velocities ensuring zero net momentum. This initial temperature creates an energetic state that will rapidly thermalize into a liquid.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L9-L11)

### Interatomic Potentials

The interaction model is defined by two commands. `pair_style lj/cut 2.5` selects the Lennard-Jones potential with a cutoff radius of 2.5 reduced distance units. This potential models the attractive van der Waals forces and short-range repulsion between atoms. The `pair_coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0 2.5` command sets the Lennard-Jones parameters (ε=1.0, σ=1.0) for interactions between type 1 atoms, with the same cutoff distance. These parameters create a standard Lennard-Jones fluid widely studied in the literature.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L13-L14)

### Neighbor List Optimization

Efficient force calculation requires managing neighbor lists. The `neighbor 0.3 bin` command establishes that atoms within 0.3 reduced distance units beyond the force cutoff should be included in neighbor lists, providing a safety buffer for atoms moving between updates. The `neigh_modify every 20 delay 0 check no` command configures rebuilding neighbor lists every 20 timesteps with no initial delay. The `check no` option disables distance checking between rebuilds for additional efficiency at the cost of accuracy—acceptable for this demonstration but something to consider carefully for production simulations.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L16-L17)

### Time Integration

The `fix 1 all nve` command applies the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble integrator to all atoms using the Velocity Verlet algorithm. This "fix" in LAMMPS terminology is an operation that modifies the system state at each timestep. The NVE ensemble conserves total energy, making it ideal for fundamental dynamics studies. The fix ID "1" allows reference to this integrator later if needed.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L19)

### Output Configuration

The `thermo 50` command instructs LAMMPS to print thermodynamic output (temperature, energy, pressure, etc.) every 50 timesteps. This provides essential monitoring of the simulation's evolution. The commented `dump` commands show alternative output methods for visualization, including atomic trajectory dumps and image generation—these are disabled by default to keep the example simple.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L25-L33)

### Running the Simulation

The `run 250` command executes 250 timesteps of molecular dynamics. Combined with the thermo output interval, this produces 6 thermodynamic snapshots capturing the system's evolution from ordered lattice to disordered liquid. The total wall time is approximately 1-2 seconds on modern processors, making it an excellent test case.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L33)

## Running LAMMPS from the Command Line

The most common way to execute LAMMPS is through the command line interface. After building LAMMPS following the [Installation and Build System](3-installation-and-build-system) instructions, you can run simulations by invoking the executable with an input script argument.

The basic execution syntax is straightforward:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Open Terminal] --> B[Navigate to Example Directory]
    B --> C[Ensure LAMMPS Executable Available]
    C --> D[Run: lmp -in in.melt]
    D --> E[Review log.lammps Output]
    E --> F[Check for dump Files]
```

Navigate to the melt example directory and execute:

```
cd examples/melt
lmp -in in.melt
```

This produces a log file (typically named `log.lammps`) containing thermodynamic data and timing information. The log file from a sample run shows the expected behavior:

```
Step Temp E_pair E_mol TotEng Press 
    0   3   -6.7733681   0   -2.2744931   -3.7033504 
   50   1.6842865   -4.8082494   0   -2.2824513   5.5666131 
  100   1.6712577   -4.7875609   0   -2.281301   5.6613913 
  150   1.6444751   -4.7471034   0   -2.2810074   5.8614211 
  200   1.6471542   -4.7509053   0   -2.2807916   5.8805431 
  250   1.6645597   -4.7774327   0   -2.2812174   5.7526089 
```

The temperature drops from the initial value of 3.0 to approximately 1.65 as kinetic energy converts to potential energy during the melting process. The total energy remains approximately constant (around -2.28), as expected for an NVE ensemble. The pressure stabilizes around 5.7 reduced pressure units, characteristic of a dense Lennard-Jones fluid.

Sources: [examples/melt/log.8Apr21.melt.g++.1](examples/melt/log.8Apr21.melt.g++.1#L44-L50)

> [!TIP]
> The log file contains critical diagnostic information beyond thermodynamics. Check the "Loop time" section for performance metrics and "Neighbor list info" for verification that neighbor list settings are appropriate for your system. Dangerous builds warnings indicate atoms moving too far between neighbor list updates, requiring adjustment of neighbor list parameters.

## Running LAMMPS as a Python Library

For programmatic control and integration with Python workflows, LAMMPS provides a Python interface that offers both convenience and flexibility. This approach enables you to embed LAMMPS simulations within larger Python scripts, access simulation data directly, and implement custom analysis workflows.

![Python Integration Example](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/python/examples/simple.py?raw=true)

The basic Python script mirrors the command-line approach:

```python
from lammps import lammps

# Create LAMMPS instance
lmp = lammps()

# Run commands one at a time
lmp.command("units lj")
lmp.command("atom_style atomic")
lmp.command("lattice fcc 0.8442")
lmp.command("region box block 0 10 0 10 0 10")
lmp.command("create_box 1 box")
lmp.command("create_atoms 1 box")
lmp.command("mass 1 1.0")
lmp.command("velocity all create 3.0 87287 loop geom")
lmp.command("pair_style lj/cut 2.5")
lmp.command("pair_coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0 2.5")
lmp.command("neighbor 0.3 bin")
lmp.command("neigh_modify every 20 delay 0 check no")
lmp.command("fix 1 all nve")
lmp.command("thermo 50")
lmp.command("run 250")
```

The Python interface provides several powerful features:

**Data Extraction**: Access atomic coordinates, velocities, and forces programmatically:

```python
# Gather all atomic coordinates
x = lmp.gather_atoms("x", 1, 3)
# Gather all forces
f = lmp.gather_atoms("f", 1, 3)
```

**Interactive Simulation Control**: Modify the simulation between runs:

```python
# Run additional steps
lmp.command("run 10")

# Extract and modify coordinates
x = lmp.gather_atoms("x", 1, 3)
x[0] += 0.1  # Move first atom
lmp.scatter_atoms("x", 1, 3, x)

# Continue simulation
lmp.command("run 1")
```

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L21-L57)

## Comparison: Command Line vs Python Interface

| Feature | Command Line | Python Interface |
|---------|--------------|------------------|
| **Ease of Use** | Simple for standard workflows | Requires programming knowledge |
| **Performance** | Minimal overhead | Slight overhead from Python |
| **Data Access** | Limited to output files | Direct access to simulation data |
| **Customization** | Input script modification only | Full Python programming capabilities |
| **Integration** | Standalone execution | Easy integration with Python ecosystem |
| **Interactive Analysis** | Post-processing only | Real-time analysis and control |

## Parallel Execution Considerations

LAMMPS is designed for efficient parallel execution using MPI. The melt example runs quickly on a single processor, but for larger simulations, parallel execution becomes essential. The syntax remains simple:

```
mpirun -np 4 lmp -in in.melt
```

This distributes the simulation across 4 MPI processes, with automatic domain decomposition. Python scripts can also run in parallel by uncommenting the mpi4py sections in the example code and launching with MPI:

```
mpirun -np 4 python simple.py in.lammps
```

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L19-L23)

## Exploring Other Example Problems

The `examples` directory contains numerous well-documented test problems demonstrating various LAMMPS capabilities. These are organized into three categories:

- **Lower-case directories**: Simple test problems for individual features (e.g., `melt`, `min`, `crack`, `balance`)
- **Upper-case directories**: More complex, application-oriented examples (e.g., `ASPHERE`, `HEAT`, `KAPPA`)
- **PACKAGES directory**: Examples specific to optional LAMMPS packages

Each example directory contains an input script (`in.*`), reference log files, and often data files or documentation. The examples README provides detailed descriptions of each problem, making them excellent learning resources.

![Examples Directory Structure](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/examples/README?raw=true)

Some recommended next examples to explore:

- `examples/min/in.min`: Demonstrates energy minimization following dynamics
- `examples/crack/in.crack`: Shows fracture mechanics with more complex boundary conditions
- `examples/balance/in.balance`: Illustrates load balancing for parallel performance

Sources: [examples/README](examples/README#L1-L100)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Issue | Symptom | Solution |
|-------|---------|----------|
| **Executable not found** | `command not found: lmp` | Ensure LAMMPS is built and executable is in PATH or use full path |
| **Missing package** | `ERROR: Unknown pair style` | Rebuild LAMMPS with required package enabled via CMake |
| **File not found** | `ERROR: Cannot open input script` | Verify working directory and file path |
| **Segfault** | Sudden termination | Check for incorrect parameters, especially cutoff distances |
| **Energy drift** | Total energy not conserved | Reduce timestep, check neighbor list settings |

## Next Steps

Congratulations on running your first LAMMPS simulation! You've now experienced the complete workflow from input script creation to output analysis. To deepen your understanding, we recommend exploring these topics in sequence:

- [Molecular Dynamics Fundamentals](8-molecular-dynamics-fundamentals) to understand the physics behind the simulations
- [Units and Dimensions](9-units-and-dimensions) to master unit systems beyond Lennard-Jones reduced units
- [Command Syntax and Structure](12-command-syntax-and-structure) to learn advanced input script features
- [Energy Minimization Algorithms](20-energy-minimization-algorithms) to explore geometry optimization techniques

The examples directory remains an invaluable resource. Each input script demonstrates specific features and techniques. Study them, modify parameters, and observe the effects—that's how expertise in molecular dynamics simulation develops.


# Latest Updates



## Recent Development Activity

The LAMMPS development project continues to evolve rapidly, with significant commits and activity in December 2025. Below is a synthesis of the most impactful recent changes affecting developers and users.

### Transparency Support in Visualization

The most notable recent enhancement is the addition of transparency support to the `dump image` command. A series of commits between December 18-19, 2025, led by [Axel Kohlmeyer](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/f3137c521d76ca6c213388cef9134af7265c1c71), implemented opacity rendering for atoms, bonds, boxes, subboxes, axes, regions, and graphics objects from fixes.

This development directly addresses [feature request #4813](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4813), where users noted that rendering large global objects like regions or walls could obscure atoms of interest. The implementation uses a dithering algorithm via the Bayer matrix approach, with recommendations for FSAA values of 0.25, 0.5, or 0.75 as documented in [commit 59d391e](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/59d391eee7e8097eb39c9d31a631f616d0f615f4).

The changes were merged through [pull request #4812](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/c4e55dc01d1feca901bb7ae52082194b6b137ce6), which also added a dedicated graphics objects fix. This is a practical improvement for researchers who need to visualize complex systems where transparency helps distinguish overlapping structures.

### Collected Small Fixes and Updates

Alongside the transparency feature, [commit a51f9ba](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/a51f9ba0e719be544293987bb3cbd9939f1b01ee) merged a collection of small fixes. These included:

- Documentation clarification for the `fix align-self` command via [PR #80](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/5e14b2de6f466df7b0bfc3aa898161abe6396d50), contributed by Jeremy FERSULA
- Removal of the deprecated `zcylinder` option from `fix wall/gran` [commit 9d36d64](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/9d36d6436e077035c5254d80b013c967d2f46e22)
- Various typo corrections and code cleanup

These incremental fixes may seem minor individually, but they collectively improve code quality and user experience. The documentation corrections, in particular, address a common pain point where unclear documentation leads to incorrect simulation setups.

## Recent Bug Fixes and Resolutions

Several important bugs were resolved in recent activity, addressing issues that affected simulation correctness and build systems.

### Compute SNAP Energy and Virial Tally Issue

A significant bug was identified and fixed regarding the `compute_snap` command. As detailed in [issue #4829](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4829), the compute was attempting to access global potential energy and virial without forcing their tally on the required timestep. This caused errors when `thermo` output was not set to run on the same step as the compute.

The fix involved adding `peflag`, `timeflag`, and `pressflag` settings to the compute's constructor, ensuring energy and virial tallies occur automatically when needed. This aligns with LAMMPS's design principle that computes requiring energy/virial information should trigger those tallies, as documented in the code comments in `integrate.cpp`.

### GPU Package Bug Fixes

Multiple GPU-related issues were resolved:

- [Issue #4712](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4712): The GPU-accelerated `born/coul/long/cs/gpu` pair style was producing incorrect forces for core-shell models, leading to simulation crashes. This was specific to the GPU variant and did not affect the reference CPU implementation.

- [Issue #4798](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4798): A CUDA illegal memory access occurred when using `package kokkos comm host`. The issue stemmed from improper handling when communication was forced to host while computations remained on device. This highlights the complexity of managing host-device synchronization in GPU-accelerated molecular dynamics codes.

### INTEL Package Monte Carlo Bug

[Issue #4801](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4801) revealed a critical bug in the INTEL-accelerated implementation of `fix atom/swap`. The fix was accepting all swap attempts regardless of energy change (Delta E), effectively breaking Monte Carlo acceptance criteria. This only occurred with INTEL acceleration enabled, while reference CPU implementations correctly applied the Metropolis acceptance probability.

The issue demonstrates the risk of acceleration paths diverging from reference implementations. Users running canonical ensemble Monte Carlo swaps with INTEL acceleration should verify they're using a version where this has been addressed.

### Hybrid Scaled Kokkos Synchronization

[Issue #4788](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4788) identified a fundamental synchronization problem in `pair_hybrid_scaled_kk`. When combining custom Kokkos-enabled pair styles that compute on GPU, the host-side code attempted to scale and sum forces without synchronizing device-to-host data transfer. This resulted in all forces being zero.

The root cause was that the Kokkos implementation was nearly identical to the non-Kokkos version, performing scaling on host data while computation remained on device. This raises broader questions about whether `hybrid/scaled/kk` should be redesigned to operate entirely on device for better performance and correctness.

## Ongoing Issues and Community Feedback

Several issues remain open, reflecting active community engagement and areas needing attention.

### SCAFACOS Build Issues

[Issue #4815](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4815) reports a linker error when building LAMMPS with the SCAFACOS module. The error involves undefined references to gfortran symbols like `_gfortran_st_rewind`, `_gfortran_transfer_character_write`, and others. This occurs because SCAFACOS links Fortran libraries that aren't properly propagated in the CMake configuration.

A workaround was documented involving manual linking of `libgfortran.so.5`, but this highlights a gap in the build system's handling of mixed-language dependencies. Users following modern build practices expect CMake to handle such dependencies automatically.

### MLIAP Interface Limitations

[Issue #4814](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4814) questions whether the `forward_exchange` function in the MLIAP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential) unified interface supports CPU execution. The user observed that systems with different atom counts behaved differently on CPU versus GPU, with GPU working correctly but CPU failing after one step for larger systems.

Similarly, [issue #4787](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4787) requests box information passing for MACELES-LAMMPS integration via MLIAP. The current interface lacks box transformation capability needed for reciprocal space operations in the LES (Local Environment Scaling) method.

### Feature Requests in Pipeline

Several feature requests indicate future development directions:

- [Issue #4803](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4803): Request to read dump files in triclinic/general format. Currently, LAMMPS can write this format and read data files in it, but dump file reading is not supported. This creates workflow friction when restarting from configurations saved in this widely-used formalism.

- [Issue #4561](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4561): Request for library API access to neighbor lists from Kokkos styles. Currently, GPU-accelerated pair styles keep neighbor lists on device with no way to access them from Python for analysis, even via device pointers.

- [Issue #4763](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4763): Suggestion to align with RDKit's Molecule JSON format for better interoperability with chemical informatics workflows.

### Longstanding Physics Bugs

Some issues have been open for extended periods, indicating complex underlying problems:

- [Issue #4611](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4611): Center of mass velocity jumps when combining `fix srd` and `fix deform`, especially when disabling the thermostat. This has implications for accurate shear flow simulations with SRD fluids.

- [Issue #4602](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4602): Velocity profile kinks near periodic boundaries when using `fix srd` with `fix deform`. The issue relates to how SRD handles particle bins crossing periodic boundaries during grid shifts.

- [Issue #4770](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4770): Incorrect kernel gradients in `ComputeRHEOVShift::correct_type_interface()`, where SPH kernel gradients were not being properly calculated because `calc_dw` was never called.

- [Issue #4717](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4717): Inconsistencies in dipolar energy between `spin/dipole/long` and `spin/dipole/cut` pair styles. The long-range version produces incorrect energies for certain spin configurations, while the cutoff version matches analytical expectations.

## Looking Ahead

The December 2025 activity reveals LAMMPS's ongoing evolution in several key areas:

1. **Visualization enhancements** making it easier to interpret complex simulation results
2. **GPU acceleration maturity** as synchronization bugs are identified and addressed
3. **Build system improvements** needed for better handling of mixed-language dependencies
4. **Machine learning integration** expanding through MLIAP and related interfaces
5. **Physics correctness** through fixes of long-standing numerical issues

The transparency support in `dump image` represents the kind of user-driven improvement that directly addresses workflow pain points. Meanwhile, the various GPU-related bug fixes highlight the challenges of maintaining correctness across multiple acceleration backends (Kokkos, INTEL, native GPU).

For developers following LAMMPS development, the repository remains highly active with contributions from both core developers and community members. Issues are being opened and resolved at a steady pace, indicating healthy project maintenance and responsiveness to user feedback.

# Issues and Feedbacks



The LAMMPS community is vocal, technical, and unforgiving when things break. Looking at recent issues and the commit history, a pattern emerges: the project faces challenges around GPU acceleration, integration with external libraries, and documentation clarity. Let's break down what users are actually complaining about and what's getting fixed.

## Recent Community Feedback

### Build System and External Dependencies

The [SCAFACOS module build failure](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4815) highlights a classic problem in large scientific software: CMake dependency handling breaks when external libraries have implicit dependencies. A user reported linker errors referencing undefined gfortran symbols when building with `-DPKG_SCAFACOS=on`. The root cause? Scafacos has Fortran components, but LAMMPS's CMake configuration doesn't explicitly link against `libgfortran`.

The workaround provided by the user is telling:

```cmake
find_library(GFORTRAN_LIBRARY NAMES libgfortran.so.5)
target_link_libraries(lammps PUBLIC ${GFORTRAN_LIBRARY})
target_link_libraries(lmp PUBLIC ${GFORTRAN_LIBRARY})
```

This should be handled automatically. The issue was opened on December 16, 2025, and remains open as of this writing. It's a friction point that affects anyone trying to integrate Scafacos for long-range electrostatics or other solver capabilities.

On the GPU side, the [CUDA 13 CUB dependency question](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4751) raises a more strategic concern. With CUB now part of CCCL and breaking changes in CUDA 13, the community is asking whether maintaining the CUB dependency in the GPU package is worth the maintenance burden. The observation that LAMMPS doesn't directly include `.cuh` files—relying only on hipCUB code—suggests the dependency may be vestigial. This is exactly the kind of technical debt decision that keeps maintainers up at night.

### GPU Acceleration Woes

GPU-related issues dominate the feedback. Three distinct problems illustrate the complexity:

1. **Hybrid/scaled/kk synchronization bug**: When using `pair_style hybrid/scaled/kk` with Kokkos-enabled pair styles running on GPU, forces computed on the device never sync back to host memory. The result? All output forces are zero. The [root cause analysis](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4788) in the issue shows the code performs scaling on host-side arrays after calling GPU compute methods, without synchronization. This is a textbook GPU programming error—expecting data transfer that never happened.

2. **Illegal memory access with Kokkos comm host**: Users running with `-pk kokkos comm host` hit CUDA errors that don't occur with `comm device`. The issue [includes detailed backtraces](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4798) showing assertions failing in Kokkos core code, with block_size mysteriously set to zero. This was closed in early December 2025, suggesting a fix was merged.

3. **CORE-SHELL model on GPU**: The [BORN/COUL/LONG/CS/GPU pair_style](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4712) produces unphysical forces in core-shell models, causing immediate simulation aborts. The non-GPU version works fine, and GPU acceleration gives a 9x speedup on benchmarks. This suggests a deep bug in the GPU implementation of the polarizable core-shell formalism. The issue was closed in December 2025, but the silence on the fix details is concerning.

### Documentation Confusion

The [fix rigid documentation issue](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4765) demonstrates how unclear specs can lead to user errors. The problem centers on whether `infile` expects unwrapped center-of-mass (COM) with non-zero image flags, or wrapped COM with correct flags. The documentation suggests unwrapped COM with flags, but the code initializes flags to zero and computes them by remapping unwrapped COM.

The user provides two mathematically equivalent approaches:
- Option 1: Wrapped COM + correct image flags
- Option 2: Unwrapped COM + zero image flags

But giving both unwrapped COM and non-zero flags leads to double-counting. The issue requests a clear recommendation—presumably Option 1, since that's what restart files use. This has been open since November 2025.

## Bug Report Quality and Community Engagement

Looking at the detailed bug reports, LAMMPS users generally provide excellent reproducible cases. The [fix atom/swap INTEL bug report](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4801) is exemplary: it includes minimal input scripts, logs with and without the `-suffix intel` flag, manual energy calculations showing the problem, and clear expected vs. actual behavior. The user demonstrates that with INTEL acceleration, 100% of swap attempts are accepted regardless of energy changes—violating the Metropolis criterion—while the reference build correctly rejects most attempts.

The [compute_snap energy tally bug](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4829), closed in January 2026, shows another pattern: edge cases in compute infrastructure. The user discovered that `compute_snap` fails when global energy and virials aren't tallied on the same timestep it's invoked. The suggested fix—adding `peflag = 1; timeflag = 1; pressflag = 1;` to the constructor—was straightforward, and the issue was quickly resolved.

## Recent Fixes and Community Wins

The commit history shows responsive development. The [transparency support for dump image](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4813) was a feature request from December 2025 that was rapidly implemented. Commits from December 18-19, 2025, including [`add support for opacity to regions and graphics from fixes`](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/5ac14d13bec7cb9bb78b02bd0026b5c7ac859a67) and [`document transparency settings`](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/6b1d4d3c73042682f7d68e7c8ecf35b920beaaf6), show the feature going in fast. This is exactly the kind of developer-facing improvement—better visualization capability—that users appreciate.

The [collected small fixes and updates](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/commit/a51f9ba0e719be544293987bb3cbd9939f1b01ee) merge on December 19, 2025, includes the transparency work plus various corrections. This pattern of bundling minor fixes is healthy for maintenance velocity.

## Recurring Themes

Based on the issue data, several themes emerge:

| Category | Open Issues | Status | Concern Level |
|----------|-------------|--------|---------------|
| GPU/CUDA bugs | 3 | Mixed (1 closed, 2 open) | High - affects performance users |
| External package integration | 2 | Both open | Medium - affects niche workflows |
| Documentation clarity | 2 | Both open | Low-medium - confusing but workable |
| Physics model correctness | 2 | Mixed (1 closed, 1 open) | High - affects scientific validity |
| Feature requests | 2 | 1 closed, 1 open | Variable |

The velocity profile issues with [fix srd and fix deform](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4611) and the associated [shear flow problems](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4602) are particularly concerning. Users report kinks in velocity profiles near periodic boundaries and vanishing profiles when the thermostat is disabled. These were closed in December 2025, but the fix details matter—SRD (Stochastic Rotation Dynamics) simulations depend critically on maintaining correct velocity profiles under shear.

## Interface and Integration Requests

Two integration requests stand out:

The [MACELES-LAMMPS-MLIAP interface issue](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4787) requests box information passing for the LES (Local Environment Scaling) transformation. The error message shows a singular matrix when attempting `linalg.inv`, suggesting the box information simply isn't available in the current MLIAP interface. This blocks a specific ML potential workflow.

The [RDKit JSON compatibility request](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4763) is more exploratory—asking whether LAMMPS's JSON spec could align with RDKit's Molecule JSON format. This shows users thinking about cross-toolchain interoperability, though it's unclear if this will lead to concrete work.

## Performance Portability Tensions

The [Kokkos neighbor list access request](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/issues/4561) exposes a fundamental tension in LAMMPS's Kokkos strategy. Kokkos neighbor lists live on device, but Python analysis workflows need host access. The user points out there's not even a way to get GPU device pointers for neighbor lists. This was opened in April 2025 and updated in October 2025, suggesting ongoing interest but no clear path forward.

The underlying problem: LAMMPS's Kokkos styles optimize for device execution, but library users need host-side data for analysis. Either you incur frequent transfers (performance cost) or you provide opaque handles (usability cost). There's no perfect solution here.

## Summary

LAMMPS users are sophisticated—they file detailed bug reports with minimal reproducers, analyze source code to identify root causes, and provide patches. The issues surface real problems: GPU bugs that produce wrong physics, build failures from implicit dependencies, and documentation that confuses more than clarifies.

The development team appears responsive, with transparency support going from feature request to implementation in under two weeks. However, the open issue list shows persistent challenges around GPU acceleration correctness and external library integration that require architectural attention.

For prospective LAMMPS users, the takeaway is clear: GPU acceleration provides speedups but introduces complexity and potential correctness issues. Build from source, test thoroughly, and consider whether your workflow requires niche integrations that may not be fully supported.

# Molecular Dynamics Fundamentals



This page explains the core computational concepts underlying molecular dynamics simulations in LAMMPS. We'll examine how LAMMPS implements the fundamental MD algorithm—from integrating equations of motion to computing forces and managing particle interactions. Understanding these fundamentals provides the foundation for exploring more advanced simulation techniques covered in subsequent documentation pages.

## The MD Simulation Loop

LAMMPS implements the classical molecular dynamics algorithm through a well-structured time integration loop. The `Verlet` class in `src/verlet.cpp` orchestrates this process, executing a sequence of operations at each timestep that advances the system's state while conserving energy and momentum.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    Start([Start Timestep]) --> InitInteg[Initial Integration<br/>Update positions]
    InitInteg --> Check{Need neighbor rebuild?}
    
    Check -->|No| ForwardComm[Forward communication<br/>Exchange ghost atom data]
    Check -->|Yes| PreEx[Pre-exchange fixes]
    PreEx --> ApplyPBC[Apply periodic boundary conditions]
    ApplyPBC --> Exchange[Exchange atoms<br/>Move atoms between processors]
    Exchange --> Border[Set up ghost atoms]
    Border --> BuildNeigh[Build neighbor lists]
    
    ForwardComm --> ForceClear[Clear forces]
    BuildNeigh --> ForceClear
    
    ForceClear --> PreForce[Pre-force fixes]
    PreForce --> PairComp[Pair style forces]
    PairComp --> BondComp[Bond forces]
    BondComp --> AngleComp[Angle forces]
    AngleComp --> DihedralComp[Dihedral forces]
    DihedralComp --> ImproperComp[Improper forces]
    ImproperComp --> KSpace[K-space/Long-range forces]
    
    KSpace --> PreRev[Pre-reverse fixes]
    PreRev --> ReverseComm[Reverse communication<br/>Sum forces from ghosts]
    ReverseComm --> PostForce[Post-force fixes]
    PostForce --> FinalInteg[Final Integration<br/>Update velocities]
    FinalInteg --> EndStep[End-of-step fixes]
    EndStep --> Output{Output due?}
    Output -->|Yes| WriteOutput[Write thermodynamics & dumps]
    Output -->|No| Continue
    WriteOutput --> Continue{More timesteps?}
    Continue -->|Yes| Start
    Continue -->|No| End([End Simulation])
```

The core integration loop resides in the `Verlet::run()` method, which iterates through timesteps performing the complete MD cycle [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L229-L360).

## Time Integration Algorithms

LAMMPS implements the **velocity Verlet** algorithm as its default integration scheme, which provides excellent energy conservation properties and time-reversibility. The algorithm splits each timestep into two half-steps for velocity updates with a position update in between.

The implementation follows this sequence:

1. **Initial half-step velocity update** (via `modify->initial_integrate()`)
2. **Full-step position update** 
3. **Force computation** at new positions
4. **Final half-step velocity update** (via `modify->final_integrate()`)

The integration classes inherit from `Integrate` [src/integrate.h](src/integrate.h), with `Verlet` providing the standard velocity Verlet implementation. Other integrators like `FixNVT`, `FixNPT`, and `FixNH` extend this pattern to implement specific ensemble thermostats and barostats.

Sources: [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L229-L360), [src/integrate.h](src/integrate.h)

## Force Computation Architecture

LAMMPS computes interatomic forces through a modular, extensible force field architecture. The `Force` class serves as the central manager, coordinating multiple types of force contributions:

| Force Type | Purpose | Key Classes | Typical Applications |
|------------|---------|-------------|---------------------|
| **Pair Styles** | Non-bonded pairwise interactions | `Pair`, subclasses | Lennard-Jones, Coulomb, Buckingham |
| **Bond Styles** | Covalent bond stretching | `Bond`, subclasses | Harmonic, FENE, Morse |
| **Angle Styles** | Three-body angle bending | `Angle`, subclasses | Harmonic, cosine |
| **Dihedral Styles** | Four-body torsional rotation | `Dihedral`, subclasses | CHARMM, OPLS |
| **Improper Styles** | Out-of-plane deformation | `Improper`, subclasses | Harmonic inversion |
| **K-Space Styles** | Long-range electrostatics | `KSpace`, subclasses | Ewald, PPPM, particle-particle |

The force initialization sequence ensures proper ordering—K-space must initialize before pair styles to define screening parameters like `g_ewald` [src/force.cpp](src/force.cpp#L176-L220).

### Force Computation Order

During each timestep, forces accumulate in this specific order:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Start[Force Computation] --> Clear[Clear forces to zero]
    Clear --> Pair[Pair style<br/>compute]
    Pair --> Bond[Bond style<br/>compute]
    Bond --> Angle[Angle style<br/>compute]
    Angle --> Dihedral[Dihedral style<br/>compute]
    Dihedral --> Improper[Improper style<br/>compute]
    Improper --> KSpace[K-space style<br/>compute]
    KSpace --> End[Force accumulation complete]
    
    style Pair fill:#e1f5ff
    style Bond fill:#fff4e1
    style Angle fill:#ffe1f5
    style Dihedral fill:#e1ffe1
    style Improper fill:#f5e1ff
    style KSpace fill:#ffe1e1
```

This ordering is critical because some bonded potentials tally pairwise energy/virial contributions that depend on pair calculations being completed first [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L310-L340).

Sources: [src/force.cpp](src/force.cpp#L176-L220), [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L310-L340)

## Neighbor List Management

Efficient force computation requires knowing which atoms interact. LAMMPS uses **neighbor lists** to track atom pairs within a cutoff distance plus a "skin" distance, avoiding O(N²) pairwise checks.

### When to Rebuild

The `Neighbor::decide()` method determines whether lists need rebuilding based on [src/neighbor.cpp](src/neighbor.cpp#L2362-L2390):

- **Delay**: Minimum timesteps between potential rebuilds
- **Every**: Check periodically after delay expires  
- **Distance check**: Verify if any atom moved more than half the skin distance

### Distance Checking Algorithm

The skin distance ensures atoms cannot move further than the skin without triggering a rebuild. For orthogonal boxes, LAMMPS checks the 8 corner displacements and conservatively reduces the effective skin distance [src/neighbor.cpp](src/neighbor.cpp#L2396-L2440):

```
effective_skin = 0.5 × (skin - (Δcorner1 + Δcorner2))
```

If atoms have moved further than this reduced distance across any processor, all processors rebuild their neighbor lists.

### Neighbor List Types

LAMMPS supports several neighbor list strategies:

| List Type | Description | Memory | Speed | Use Case |
|-----------|-------------|--------|-------|----------|
| **Half** | Store i-j pairs once (i < j) | Lower | Slower | Most common |
| **Full** | Store both i-j and j-i | Higher | Faster | Many-body potentials |
| **Multi** | Multiple lists at different cutoffs | Variable | Optimized | Multi-scale interactions |
| **Granular** | Specialized for particle contacts | Optimized | Efficient | Granular materials |

> [!TIP]
> The neighbor skin parameter (`neigh modify skin`) balances performance: larger skins reduce rebuild frequency but increase computation per timestep. Optimal values depend on particle velocities and system density.

Sources: [src/neighbor.cpp](src/neighbor.cpp#L2362-L2460)

## Periodic Boundary Conditions

Molecular dynamics simulations typically model bulk materials rather than isolated clusters. LAMMPS implements **periodic boundary conditions** (PBC) that simulate infinite systems by replicating the simulation box in all directions.

When an atom crosses a box face, it re-enters from the opposite face, maintaining particle number and density. The communication system handles three key tasks:

1. **Exchange**: Move atoms that have left the local processor's domain to neighboring processors
2. **Borders**: Create ghost atoms near processor boundaries for force calculations  
3. **Reverse**: Sum force contributions from ghost atoms back to their owners

The domain transformation handles both orthogonal and **triclinic** boxes through coordinate transformations (`x2lamda` and `lamda2x`) when necessary [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L272-L285).

Sources: [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L262-L290)

## Communication and Parallelization

LAMMPS uses spatial domain decomposition for parallel efficiency. The simulation volume is partitioned among processors, with each processor responsible for atoms in its subdomain. This requires:

### Forward Communication
After position updates, processors send updated positions to neighbors to maintain consistent ghost atom data [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L259-L260).

### Reverse Communication  
After force computation, forces computed on ghost atoms are summed back to their owner processors. This uses Newton's third law to avoid double-counting when `newton` flag is enabled [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L335-L338).

> [!TIP]
> Use `comm_modify mode` to choose between communication strategies: 'single' sends messages one neighbor at a time (lower latency), while 'multi' buffers all communications together (higher bandwidth utilization).

## The Modify System: Hooks for Customization

LAMMPS provides extensive customization through the `Modify` system, which executes user-defined operations at specific points in the timestep [src/modify.cpp](src/modify.cpp). These "hooks" allow adding:

| Hook Point | Timing | Typical Uses |
|------------|--------|--------------|
| `initial_integrate` | After position update | Thermostats, constraints |
| `post_integrate` | After position update, before comm | Velocity modifications |
| `pre_neighbor` | Before neighbor list build | Pair style overrides |
| `post_neighbor` | After neighbor list build | List processing |
| `pre_force` | Before force computation | Force field modifications |
| `post_force` | After force computation | External forces, constraints |
| `final_integrate` | After velocity update | Thermostats, constraints |
| `end_of_step` | At timestep end | Analysis, property calculation |

This modular design enables complex simulation protocols without modifying the core integration loop.

Sources: [src/modify.cpp](src/modify.cpp#L401-L503)

## Output and Analysis

The `Output` class manages simulation output, including thermodynamic quantities and trajectory files [src/output.cpp](src/output.cpp#L354-L487):

- **Thermodynamics**: Instantaneous properties (temperature, pressure, energy) printed at specified intervals
- **Dump files**: Atom coordinates, velocities, and custom properties for visualization and analysis
- **Restart files**: Complete simulation state for continuation or checkpointing

Output timing follows the main loop, occurring after all timestep operations complete [src/verlet.cpp](src/verlet.cpp#L350-L356).

Sources: [src/output.cpp](src/output.cpp#L354-L487)

## Core Architecture Overview

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Main LAMMPS Objects"
        Update[Update<br/>Time & integration]
        Atom[Atom<br/>Particle data]
        Force[Force<br/>Force field]
        Neighbor[Neighbor<br/>Pair lists]
        Modify[Modify<br/>Fixes & computes]
        Comm[Comm<br/>Parallel communication]
        Domain[Domain<br/>Boundary conditions]
        Output[Output<br/>Results writing]
    end
    
    Update --> Integrate[Integrate<br/>Verlet algorithm]
    Integrate --> |positions| Atom
    Integrate --> |forces| Force
    Force --> |cutoff| Neighbor
    Neighbor --> |pairs| Force
    Force --> |modify| Modify
    Modify --> |hooks| Integrate
    Atom --> |exchange| Comm
    Comm --> |ghosts| Neighbor
    Domain --> |PBC| Comm
    Integrate --> |properties| Output
    
    style Update fill:#e3f2fd
    style Integrate fill:#bbdefb
    style Atom fill:#c8e6c9
    style Force fill:#ffccbc
    style Neighbor fill:#d1c4e9
    style Modify fill:#f8bbd9
    style Comm fill:#b2dfdb
    style Output fill:#fff9c4
```

This architecture demonstrates LAMMPS's object-oriented design, where each component has clear responsibilities while working together through well-defined interfaces.
