# Boundary Conditions and Periodic Systems



This page comprehensively documents LAMMPS's sophisticated boundary condition and periodic system architecture. Understanding these concepts is fundamental to molecular dynamics simulations, as boundary conditions define how simulation boxes interact with their surroundings and how atoms interact across periodic boundaries.

## Boundary Condition Architecture

LAMMPS implements boundary conditions through the **Domain** class, which serves as the central manager for all simulation box geometries and boundary specifications. The architecture provides flexible support for periodic, fixed, and shrink-wrap boundaries across all three dimensions.

The boundary system is built around a `boundary[3][2]` array that stores boundary settings for each dimension (x, y, z) and each side (low, high). Each boundary can be configured with one of four modes:

| Boundary Type | Code | Description | Use Case |
|---------------|------|-------------|----------|
| Periodic | 0 | Atoms wrap across boundary | Bulk materials, periodic crystals |
| Fixed | 1 | Reflective/inert wall | Surfaces, isolated systems |
| Shrink-wrap | 2 | Box shrinks to fit atoms | Droplets, clusters |
| Shrink-wrap with minimum | 3 | Shrinks with minimum size constraint | Flexible volume calculations |

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Domain {
        +int boundary[3][2]
        +int xperiodic, yperiodic, zperiodic
        +int triclinic
        +double boxlo[3], boxhi[3]
        +double xy, xz, yz
        +double h[6], h_inv[6]
        +void pbc()
        +void set_boundary()
        +void remap()
        +void minimum_image()
    }
    
    class Atom {
        +double** x
        +imageint* image
        +double** v
    }
    
    Domain --> Atom : manages
```

The boundary configuration is initialized with periodic boundaries by default, as shown in the Domain constructor where all six boundary faces are set to periodic (0) [src/domain.cpp#L77-L79](src/domain.cpp#L77-L79). The `set_boundary()` method processes boundary specifications from input scripts, ensuring consistency and validating that both sides of a dimension must be periodic if either is periodic [src/domain.cpp#L2090-L2163](src/domain.cpp#L2090-L2163).

Sources: [src/domain.h#L36-L40](src/domain.h#L36-L40), [src/domain.cpp#L64-L120](src/domain.cpp#L64-L120)

## Periodic Boundary Conditions

Periodic boundary conditions (PBC) are the cornerstone of bulk material simulations, creating an infinite system from a finite simulation cell. LAMMPS implements PBC through a sophisticated combination of coordinate wrapping, image flag management, and minimum image conventions.

### PBC Application Algorithm

The core PBC algorithm operates in `Domain::pbc()` [src/domain.cpp#L769-L887](src/domain.cpp#L769-L887), which processes each owned atom to ensure it remains within the simulation box. For atoms crossing boundaries, the algorithm performs three critical operations:

1. **Coordinate Wrapping**: Atoms leaving the box are repositioned on the opposite side by adding or subtracting the box period
2. **Image Flag Update**: Encoded image flags track how many times each atom has crossed periodic boundaries
3. **Velocity Remapping**: When box deformation occurs, velocities are adjusted to maintain physical consistency

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Atom at Position x] --> B{Inside Box Bounds?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Keep Position]
    B -->|No, x < lo| D[Add Period to Coordinate]
    B -->|No, x >= hi| E[Subtract Period from Coordinate]
    D --> F[Decrement Image Flag]
    E --> G[Increment Image Flag]
    F --> H[Apply Velocity Remapping if Needed]
    G --> H
    H --> I[Final Position in Box]
    C --> I
```

The image flag system uses a compact bit-packed encoding where each dimension uses 10 bits to store image counts [src/domain.h#L188-L200](src/domain.h#L188-L200). This allows tracking of boundary crossings up to 512 times in either direction per dimension, which is essential for accurate bond calculations and topology maintenance.

> [!TIP]
> When atoms cross periodic boundaries during dynamics, their image flags are updated to track the cumulative number of crossings. This is critical for maintaining molecular topology when bonded molecules span multiple periodic images.

### Minimum Image Convention

LAMMPS implements the minimum image convention to ensure atoms interact with their nearest periodic images. The `minimum_image()` method [src/domain.cpp#L1222-L1297](src/domain.cpp#L1222-L1297) adjusts distance vectors by adding or subtracting box periods until the distance is within half the box size in each dimension.

For orthogonal boxes, this is straightforward:
```
if (fabs(dx) > xprd_half) {
    if (dx < 0.0) dx += xprd;
    else dx -= xprd;
}
```

For triclinic boxes, the algorithm becomes more complex because changing one dimension's periodic image affects coordinates in other dimensions due to tilt factors [src/domain.cpp#L1258-L1296](src/domain.cpp#L1258-L1296). This ensures proper handling of interactions in sheared systems.

> [!TIP]
> The minimum image convention assumes the simulation box is large enough that no atom interacts with more than its nearest periodic image. Violations of this assumption can lead to unphysical interactions and should be detected by careful analysis of potential cutoffs relative to box dimensions.

Sources: [src/domain.cpp#L769-L887](src/domain.cpp#L769-L887), [src/domain.cpp#L1222-L1297](src/domain.cpp#L1222-L1297)

## Triclinic Box Systems

LAMMPS supports two types of triclinic boxes: restricted and general triclinic. These allow simulation of sheared systems, crystals with low-symmetry unit cells, and systems undergoing deformation.

### Restricted Triclinic Boxes

Restricted triclinic boxes are characterized by three tilt factors (xy, xz, yz) that define the skew of the simulation box. The shape matrix H in Voigt notation [src/domain.h#L87-L88](src/domain.h#L87-L88) describes the transformation:

```
H = [xx   xy   xz]
    [0    yy   yz]
    [0    0    zz]
```

This restricted form ensures the box can be continuously deformed from an orthogonal box without topological changes. The domain stores both the tilt factors and the complete shape matrix H and its inverse H_inv for efficient coordinate transformations [src/domain.h#L86-L88](src/domain.h#L86-L88).

### General Triclinic Boxes

General triclinic boxes support arbitrary edge vectors defined by three vectors: a, b, and c. This is useful for directly specifying complex crystal structures without intermediate transformations. The `define_general_triclinic()` method [src/domain.cpp#L553-L598](src/domain.cpp#L553-L598) accepts arbitrary edge vectors and computes a rotation to convert to restricted triclinic representation.

The conversion involves quaternion-based rotation calculations that transform the general triclinic box to the restricted form [src/domain.cpp#L607-L676](src/domain.cpp#L607-L676). This enables LAMMPS to use its optimized restricted triclinic algorithms while accepting general box specifications.

### Lambda Coordinate System

For efficient computation in triclinic boxes, LAMMPS uses a fractional (lambda) coordinate system where coordinates range from 0 to 1 in each dimension. Coordinate transformations between Cartesian and lambda coordinates use the shape matrix:

```
x = H * lamda + boxlo
lamda = H^(-1) * (x - boxlo)
```

The `lamda2x()` [src/domain.cpp#L2212-L2221](src/domain.cpp#L2212-L2221) and `x2lamda()` [src/domain.cpp#L2241-L2255](src/domain.cpp#L2241-L2255) methods implement these transformations for all atoms, while overloaded versions handle individual atoms [src/domain.cpp#L2282-L2305](src/domain.cpp#L2282-L2305). Using lambda coordinates simplifies periodic boundary checks and improves computational efficiency for many operations.

Sources: [src/domain.cpp#L553-L676](src/domain.cpp#L553-L676), [src/domain.cpp#L2212-L2320](src/domain.cpp#L2212-L2320)

## Coordinate Remapping and Unmapping

Coordinate remapping ensures atoms remain within the simulation box during and after operations that might move them outside. LAMMPS provides several remapping methods for different use cases:

### Remap Methods

- **remap(double *x, imageint &image)** [src/domain.cpp#L1550-L1630](src/domain.cpp#L1550-L1630): Remaps a single coordinate while updating image flags
- **remap(double *x)** [src/domain.cpp#L1640-L1677](src/domain.cpp#L1640-L1677): Remaps without image flag calculation (useful for post-processing)
- **remap_all()** [src/domain.cpp#L1689-L1696](src/domain.cpp#L1689-L1696): Remaps all atoms in the system
- **remap_near()** [src/domain.cpp#L1704-L1776](src/domain.cpp#L1704-L1776): Remaps to within half box length of a reference position

The remapping algorithm iteratively adds or subtracts box periods until coordinates are within the box bounds [src/domain.cpp#L1570-L1627](src/domain.cpp#L1570-L1627). For triclinic boxes, coordinates are first converted to lambda space, remapped, then converted back to Cartesian coordinates.

### Unmapping Operations

Unmapping performs the inverse operation, reconstructing the original absolute position from a boxed coordinate and its image flags. The `unmap()` methods [src/domain.cpp#L1801-L1825](src/domain.cpp#L1801-L1825) apply image flag offsets to recover the unwrapped position, which is essential for calculating mean-squared displacement and other diffusive properties.

Sources: [src/domain.cpp#L1550-L1825](src/domain.cpp#L1550-L1825)

## Box Boundary Management

The boundary system provides comprehensive management of simulation box evolution through several key mechanisms.

### Boundary String Representation

The `boundary_string()` method [src/domain.cpp#L2192-L2200](src/domain.cpp#L2192-L2200) generates a human-readable string representation of the boundary settings. For example, "p p p" represents fully periodic boundaries, while "p f f" represents periodic in x but fixed in y and z.

### Box Change Tracking

LAMMPS tracks three types of box changes through flags [src/domain.h#L100-L103](src/domain.h#L100-L103):

- **box_change_size**: Box dimensions change
- **box_change_shape**: Box tilt factors change  
- **box_change_domain**: Processor sub-domains change

These flags are set by fixes and other operations that modify the box, triggering necessary communication and data structure updates. The `init()` method [src/domain.cpp#L136-L150](src/domain.cpp#L136-L150) queries all fixes to determine if any will cause box changes.

### Shrink-wrap Boundaries

Shrink-wrap boundaries automatically adjust box dimensions to contain atoms. The domain stores minimum box sizes `minxlo`, `minxhi`, etc. [src/domain.h#L71-L73](src/domain.h#L71-L73) that constrain how small the box can become. The `box_too_small_check()` [src/domain.cpp#L1071-L1183](src/domain.cpp#L1071-L1183) and `subbox_too_small_check()` [src/domain.cpp#L1184-L1220](src/domain.cpp#L1184-L1220) methods validate that boxes remain large enough for communication and neighbor calculations.

Sources: [src/domain.h#L71-L103](src/domain.h#L71-L103), [src/domain.cpp#L136-L150](src/domain.cpp#L136-L150)

## Practical Implementation Examples

The LAMMPS examples directory provides practical demonstrations of boundary condition usage in various scenarios.

### Orthogonal FCC Lattice

The orthogonal box example [examples/triclinic/in.fcc.orthog](examples/triclinic/in.fcc.orthog) demonstrates a simple periodic system:

```
lattice       fcc 1.1
region        mybox block 0 1 0 1 0 1
create_box    1 mybox
create_atoms  1 box
```

This creates a face-centered cubic lattice with fully periodic boundaries, suitable for bulk crystal simulations.

### General Triclinic Box

The general triclinic example [examples/triclinic/in.data.general](examples/triclinic/in.data.general) shows how to read and work with complex box geometries:

```
read_data     data.general
pair_style    lj/cut 1.2
thermo_style  custom step pe avecx avecy avecz bvecx bvecy bvecz &
                cvecx cvecy cvecz pxx pyy pzz vol
thermo_modify triclinic/general yes
```

The `thermo_modify triclinic/general yes` directive ensures thermo output uses the general triclinic representation.

Sources: [examples/triclinic/in.fcc.orthog](examples/triclinic/in.fcc.orthog), [examples/triclinic/in.data.general](examples/triclinic/in.data.general)

## Integration with Simulation Components

The boundary condition system integrates deeply with LAMMPS's other core components:

### Communication System

The parallel communication system relies on boundary information to determine which atoms to exchange between processors. Sub-domain boundaries are stored in `sublo` and `subhi` arrays [src/domain.h#L77-L77](src/domain.h#L77-L77) and are updated when the global box changes.

### Neighbor Lists

Neighbor list construction uses the minimum image convention to ensure proper interaction detection across periodic boundaries. The `minimum_image_check()` inline method [src/domain.h#L194-L200](src/domain.h#L194-L200) provides fast checking for potential image flag violations.

### Data Input/Output

The domain system supports writing boundary and box information to data files. The `print_box()` method [src/domain.cpp#L2169-L2185](src/domain.cpp#L2169-L2185) generates formatted output showing either orthogonal or triclinic box specifications.

## Advanced Topics

### Deformation and Velocity Remapping

When using box deformation (e.g., through `fix deform`), the domain tracks deformation flags `deform_flag`, `deform_vremap`, and `deform_groupbit` [src/domain.h#L105-L107](src/domain.h#L105-L107). During PBC application, velocities are remapped according to the box deformation rate tensor `h_rate` [src/domain.cpp#L810-L826](src/domain.cpp#L810-L826), ensuring atoms acquire the appropriate velocity due to box motion.

### Image Flag Consistency

When boundary conditions change from periodic to non-periodic, the domain automatically resets image flags for the affected dimensions [src/domain.cpp#L2145-L2162](src/domain.cpp#L2145-L2162). A warning is issued if any atoms had non-zero image flags in dimensions that become non-periodic, alerting users to potential topology issues.

Sources: [src/domain.cpp#L2145-L2162](src/domain.cpp#L2145-L2162)

## Summary and Best Practices

LAMMPS's boundary condition and periodic system architecture provides a robust foundation for diverse simulation scenarios. Key best practices include:

1. **Box Size Planning**: Ensure box dimensions are at least twice the potential cutoff in each periodic dimension to satisfy minimum image requirements
2. **Triclinic Considerations**: When using triclinic boxes, be aware that tilt factors affect effective box dimensions in other directions
3. **Image Flag Tracking**: Monitor image flags for molecules that span periodic boundaries, especially during topology changes
4. **Boundary Consistency**: Use shrink-wrap boundaries judiciously as they can cause box fluctuations that affect thermodynamic properties

For more details on related topics, see [Command Syntax and Structure](12-command-syntax-and-structure) for how to specify boundaries in input scripts, [Neighbor Lists](19-long-range-electrostatics-and-k-space-methods) for how periodic boundaries affect neighbor construction, and [Replica Exchange Methods](23-replica-exchange-methods) for advanced boundary condition applications.

# Command Syntax and Structure



This page explains the fundamental syntax and structure of LAMMPS input scripts, providing the foundation for writing effective molecular dynamics simulations. Understanding command structure is essential before progressing to more advanced topics like [Variables and Control Flow](13-variables-and-control-flow) and simulation techniques.

## Input Script Fundamentals

LAMMPS input scripts are plain text files read line by line during simulation execution. Each line contains a command that instructs LAMMPS to perform a specific operation. The script serves as a complete recipe for your simulation, from system setup through data output. Commands are processed sequentially, building your simulation one component at a time.

![LAMMPS Input Script Structure](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/examples/melt/in.melt?raw=true)

A typical input script follows a logical progression: define units → specify atom style → create simulation box → populate with atoms → define interactions → set integration method → configure output → run simulation. This structure is evident in the basic melt example [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1-L34), which demonstrates a complete 3D Lennard-Jones simulation setup.

## Command Syntax Basics

### Command Format

Every LAMMPS command follows this general pattern:

```
command_name keyword arguments...
```

Commands consist of a required command identifier followed by optional keywords and arguments. The command name is always first and specifies what operation to perform. Keywords modify command behavior, while arguments provide numerical or string values needed for the operation.

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L3-L4), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L3-L4)

### Comments

Comments begin with the `#` character and continue to the end of the line. Comments are ignored during execution and are essential for documenting your script logic. Most example scripts include descriptive headers explaining the simulation purpose:

```
# 3d Lennard-Jones melt
# Solvated 5-mer peptide
# 2d indenter simulation
```

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L1), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L1)

### Line Continuation

Long commands can span multiple lines using the `&` character at the end of a line. This is particularly common for complex `fix` or `dump` commands with many parameters:

```
dump 2 all image 25 image.*.jpg type type &
      axes yes 0.8 0.02 view 60 -30
```

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L20-L21), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L25-L26)

## Command Categories

Based on the examination of example scripts, LAMMPS commands can be organized into several functional categories:

### Simulation Setup Commands

These commands establish the fundamental simulation framework:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `units` | Define unit system | `units lj`, `units real` |
| `atom_style` | Specify atom attributes | `atom_style atomic`, `atom_style full` |
| `dimension` | Set spatial dimensions | `dimension 2`, `dimension 3` |
| `boundary` | Define boundary conditions | `boundary p p p`, `boundary f f p` |

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L3-L4), [examples/min/in.min](examples/min/in.min#L2-L3), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L1-L2), [examples/balance/in.balance](examples/balance/in.balance#L7-L8)

### System Creation Commands

Commands for building the atomic system:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `lattice` | Define lattice structure | `lattice fcc 0.8442`, `lattice hex 0.9` |
| `region` | Define geometric regions | `region box block 0 10 0 10 0 10` |
| `create_box` | Create simulation box | `create_box 1 box` |
| `create_atoms` | Generate atoms | `create_atoms 1 box`, `create_atoms 0 box mol cychex 734594` |
| `read_data` | Load system from data file | `read_data data.peptide` |
| `mass` | Set atomic masses | `mass 1 1.0`, `mass 1 14.027` |

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L5-L7), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L8), [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L8-L13), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L9-L10)

### Force Field Commands

Commands defining interatomic interactions:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `pair_style` | Pair interaction method | `pair_style lj/cut 2.5`, `pair_style lj/charmm/coul/long 8.0 10.0 10.0` |
| `pair_coeff` | Pair interaction parameters | `pair_coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0 2.5` |
| `pair_modify` | Modify pair settings | `pair_modify shift yes`, `pair_modify mix geometric tail yes` |
| `bond_style` | Bond interaction method | `bond_style harmonic` |
| `angle_style` | Angle interaction method | `angle_style charmm`, `angle_style harmonic` |
| `dihedral_style` | Dihedral interaction method | `dihedral_style charmm`, `dihedral_style harmonic` |
| `improper_style` | Improper interaction method | `improper_style harmonic` |
| `kspace_style` | Long-range solver | `kspace_style pppm 0.0001` |

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L12-L13), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L4-L7), [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L5-L8), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L21-L22)

### Group and Selection Commands

Commands for organizing atoms into groups:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `group` | Define atom groups | `group peptide type <= 12`, `group mobile subtract all lower` |
| `set` | Set atom properties | `set group lower type 2` |
| `region` | Define spatial regions | `region circle sphere $(v_d/2+1) $(v_d/2/sqrt(3.0)+1) 0.0 $(v_d/2)` |

Sources: [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L17), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L26-L27), [examples/rigid/in.rigid](examples/rigid/in.rigid#L11-L19), [examples/balance/in.balance](examples/balance/in.balance#L13)

### Integration and Dynamics Commands

Commands controlling time evolution:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `velocity` | Set initial velocities | `velocity all create 3.0 87287 loop geom` |
| `fix` | Apply operations during run | `fix 1 all nve`, `fix 1 all nvt temp 275.0 275.0 100.0` |
| `unfix` | Remove a fix | `unfix 4` |
| `timestep` | Set integration timestep | `timestep 0.003`, `timestep 2.0` |
| `run` | Execute dynamics | `run 250`, `run 10000` |
| `minimize` | Perform energy minimization | `minimize 1.0e-6 0.001 1000 10000` |

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L10-L11-L32), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L14-L18-L43), [examples/min/in.min](examples/min/in.min#L14-L17-L41), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L30-L43-L69)

### Output Commands

Commands for monitoring and storing simulation data:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `thermo` | Set thermo output frequency | `thermo 50`, `thermo 100` |
| `thermo_style` | Define thermo output format | `thermo_style multi`, `thermo_style custom step temp epair press` |
| `thermo_modify` | Modify thermo settings | `thermo_modify temp new` |
| `dump` | Write atom coordinates | `dump 1 all atom 50 dump.melt` |
| `dump_modify` | Modify dump settings | `dump_modify 2 pad 3` |

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L31), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L15-L16), [examples/balance/in.balance](examples/balance/in.balance#L48-L50)

### Neighbor List Commands

Commands controlling neighbor list construction:

| Command | Purpose | Example |
|---------|---------|---------|
| `neighbor` | Set neighbor list parameters | `neighbor 0.3 bin`, `neighbor 2.0 bin` |
| `neigh_modify` | Modify neighbor list settings | `neigh_modify every 20 delay 0 check no`, `neigh_modify exclude group clump1 clump1` |

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L15-L16), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L10-L11), [examples/rigid/in.rigid](examples/rigid/in.rigid#L22-L30)

## Variable System

LAMMPS supports variables that enhance script flexibility and enable parameter sweeps. Variables are defined using the `variable` command and referenced using `$name` or `${name}` syntax.

### Variable Definition

```
variable x index 50
variable k equal 1000.0/xlat
variable y equal "13.0*ylat - step*dt*0.02*ylat"
variable boxlen index 4.0
```

Sources: [examples/balance/in.balance](examples/balance/in.balance#L4-L8), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L44-L45), [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L10)

### Variable Usage

Variables can be used in commands by preceding the variable name with `$`:

```
region box block -${boxlen} ${boxlen} -${boxlen} ${boxlen} -${boxlen} ${boxlen} units lattice
fix 4 all indent $k sphere 10 v_y 0 5.0
```

Sources: [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L11), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L46)

> [!TIP]
> Variables enable powerful parameter sweeps and automated analysis. Use `index` style variables for lists of values and `equal` style variables for computed expressions that update during simulation.

## Script Architecture and Execution Flow

Understanding how LAMMPS processes input scripts is crucial for writing efficient simulations. The following diagram illustrates the typical command flow and execution model:

```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Start([LAMMPS Start]) --> ReadScript[Read Input Script]
    ReadScript --> Parse[Parse Commands Sequentially]
    
    Parse --> SetupPhase{Setup Phase}
    
    SetupPhase --> Units[units - Define Unit System]
    Units --> AtomStyle[atom_style - Specify Atom Attributes]
    AtomStyle --> Lattice[lattice - Define Crystal Structure]
    Lattice --> Region[region - Define Simulation Box]
    Region --> CreateBox[create_box - Create Simulation Box]
    CreateBox --> CreateAtoms["create_atoms/read_data - Populate System"]
    CreateAtoms --> Mass[mass - Set Atomic Masses]
    
    Mass --> ForceField{Force Field Setup}
    ForceField --> PairStyle[pair_style - Pair Interactions]
    PairStyle --> BondAngle["bond_style, angle_style, dihedral_style"]
    BondAngle --> PairCoeff[pair_coeff - Interaction Parameters]
    PairCoeff --> KSpace[kspace_style - Long-range Solver]
    
    KSpace --> Dynamics{Dynamics Setup}
    Dynamics --> Velocity[velocity - Initial Velocities]
    Velocity --> Fix[fix - Integrator and Constraints]
    Fix --> Neighbor[neighbor - Neighbor Lists]
    Neighbor --> Timestep[timestep - Integration Step]
    
    Timestep --> Output{Output Configuration}
    Output --> Thermo[thermo - Thermodynamic Output]
    Thermo --> Dump[dump - Trajectory Output]
    
    Dump --> RunPhase{Run Phase}
    RunPhase --> Execute["run/minimize - Execute Simulation"]
    Execute --> Update[Update System State]
    Update --> CheckConvergence{Converged/Complete?}
    CheckConvergence -->|No| Execute
    CheckConvergence -->|Yes| Cleanup
    
    Cleanup[Final Output and Cleanup] --> End([Simulation Complete])
    
    style SetupPhase fill:#e1f5fe
    style ForceField fill:#f3e5f5
    style Dynamics fill:#e8f5e9
    style Output fill:#fff3e0
    style RunPhase fill:#fce4ec
    style Cleanup fill:#e0e0e0
```

This architecture shows how LAMMPS builds simulations incrementally. Each command type operates on the simulation state created by previous commands. The setup phase establishes the physical framework, the force field phase defines interactions, the dynamics phase configures integration, and the run phase performs the actual simulation.

## Common Script Patterns

### Basic Molecular Dynamics Simulation

The simplest complete script structure follows this pattern:

```
# 1. Define units and atom style
units lj
atom_style atomic

# 2. Create system
lattice fcc 0.8442
region box block 0 10 0 10 0 10
create_box 1 box
create_atoms 1 box

# 3. Define interactions
pair_style lj/cut 2.5
pair_coeff 1 1 1.0 1.0 2.5

# 4. Set up dynamics
velocity all create 3.0 87287 loop geom
fix 1 all nve

# 5. Configure output
thermo 50

# 6. Run simulation
run 250
```

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L1-L34)

### Energy Minimization

For finding stable configurations, scripts include a minimization phase:

```
# Setup system...

# Minimization
minimize 1.0e-6 0.001 1000 10000
```

Sources: [examples/min/in.min](examples/min/in.min#L41)

### Multi-stage Simulations

Complex simulations often have multiple run phases with different conditions:

```
# Phase 1: with indenter
fix 4 all indent $k sphere 10 v_y 0 5.0
run 30000

# Phase 2: without indenter
unfix 4
run 30000
```

Sources: [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L46-L69)

### Complex Systems with Constraints

More advanced systems use groups and specialized fixes:

```
# Define constrained regions
region 1 block INF INF INF 1.25 INF INF
group lower region 1
group mobile subtract all lower
set group lower type 2

# Apply constraints
fix 2 lower setforce 0.0 0.0 0.0
fix 3 all temp/rescale 100 0.1 0.1 0.01 1.0
```

Sources: [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L18-L19-L26-L34-L35)

## Script Organization Best Practices

Based on the example scripts examined, effective LAMMPS scripts follow these organizational principles:

### Logical Sectioning

Organize commands into logical blocks with descriptive comments:

```
# 1. Simulation setup
units real
atom_style full

# 2. Force field definition
pair_style lj/charmm/coul/long 8.0 10.0 10.0
bond_style harmonic

# 3. System creation
read_data data.peptide

# 4. Dynamics setup
fix 1 all nvt temp 275.0 275.0 100.0

# 5. Output configuration
thermo 50
```

Sources: [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L1-L18-L20)

### Parameter Organization

Group related parameters together for readability:

```
# LJ potentials
pair_style lj/cut 2.5
pair_coeff * * 1.0 1.0 2.5

# define groups
region 1 block INF INF INF 1.25 INF INF
group lower region 1
group mobile subtract all lower
```

Sources: [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L20-L27)

### Conditional Execution

Use comments to control optional features:

```
#dump 1 all atom 100 dump.min
#dump 2 all image 50 image.*.jpg type type &
#      zoom 1.6 adiam 1.5
```

Sources: [examples/min/in.min](examples/min/in.min#L19-L21)

## Advanced Syntax Features

### Compute References

Commands can reference computed values:

```
compute new mobile temp
velocity mobile create 0.2 482748 temp new
thermo_modify temp new
```

Sources: [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L28-L29-L50)

### Molecule Templates

Complex molecules can be defined as templates:

```
molecule cychex cyclohexane.mol
atom_style template cychex
create_atoms 0 box mol cychex 734594
```

Sources: [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L4-L5-L14)

### Hybrid Atom Styles

Multiple atom styles can be combined:

```
molecule twomols h2o.mol co2.mol offset 2 1 1 0 0
atom_style hybrid template twomols charge
```

Sources: [examples/template/in.hybrid](examples/template/in.hybrid#L2-L3)

## Command Precedence and Dependencies

The order of commands is critical because many commands depend on state established by previous commands. Understanding these dependencies prevents common errors:

1. **Units must be defined first** - All physical quantities use the specified units
2. **Atom style must precede atom creation** - Determines what atom attributes are available
3. **System creation before interactions** - Pair styles need atoms to exist
4. **Groups before group operations** - Groups must be defined before use
5. **Fixes before run** - Integration methods must be active during dynamics

Sources: All examples demonstrate this ordering consistently: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt), [examples/peptide/in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide), [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent)

> [!TIP]
> The LAMMPS manual provides detailed command-specific ordering requirements. Always verify dependencies for new commands before inserting them into existing scripts.

## Error Prevention and Debugging

Common syntax errors can be avoided by following these patterns:

### Verify Command Syntax

Each command has a specific syntax. Incorrect argument counts or types will cause errors:

```
# Correct
pair_style lj/cut 2.5

# Incorrect - wrong number of arguments
pair_style lj/cut
```

### Check Group Definitions

Ensure groups are defined before use:

```
# Correct sequence
group mobile type 1
velocity mobile create 1.0 12345

# Incorrect - undefined group
velocity mobile create 1.0 12345
group mobile type 1
```

Sources: [examples/indent/in.indent](examples/indent/in.indent#L26-L28)

### Validate Parameter Ranges

Many commands have parameter constraints. Use appropriate cutoff values and ensure physical parameters are reasonable:

```
neighbor 0.3 bin
pair_style lj/cut 2.5  # Cutoff must be > neighbor distance + skin
```

Sources: [examples/melt/in.melt](examples/melt/in.melt#L15-L12)

## Next Steps

With command syntax fundamentals established, you can explore more advanced topics:

- [Variables and Control Flow](13-variables-and-control-flow) - Learn about loops, conditionals, and advanced variable usage
- [Reading and Writing Data Files](14-reading-and-writing-data-files) - Understand data file formats and I/O operations
- [Energy Minimization Algorithms](20-energy-minimization-algorithms) - Explore minimization techniques in depth
- [Pair Styles Overview](16-pair-styles-overview) - Comprehensive guide to interatomic potentials

For practical examples, explore the extensive [examples/](examples/) directory which contains working scripts for diverse simulation scenarios including molecular systems [examples/peptide/](examples/peptide/), rigid bodies [examples/rigid/](examples/rigid/), and specialized techniques [examples/indent/](examples/indent/).

# Variables and Control Flow



LAMMPS provides a powerful scripting language for managing simulation parameters and controlling execution flow through variables and control structures. This document covers the fundamentals of variable definition, substitution patterns, and control flow constructs that enable flexible and dynamic simulation scripts.

## Variable Types and Definition

LAMMPS supports multiple variable types that serve different purposes in simulation scripts. The basic syntax for defining variables follows the pattern `variable name style value`, where the style determines the variable's behavior and usage context.

**Index Variables** are the simplest form, storing a single value that can be substituted directly:

```
variable boxlen index 4.0
region box block -${boxlen} ${boxlen} -${boxlen} ${boxlen} -${boxlen} ${boxlen} units lattice
```
Sources: [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L10-L11)

**Equal Variables** store computed expressions and are evaluated each time they're referenced. They can contain mathematical formulas and reference other variables:

```
variable density equal 1.0
variable kT equal 0.05
variable deltamove equal 0.1
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L3-L5)

**Loop Variables** work with the `next` and `jump` commands to implement iteration:

```
variable iter loop 3000
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L2)

**Atom Variables** allow per-atom property calculations and manipulations:

```
variable xnew equal x[v_i]+v_deltamove*random(-1.0,1.0,${seed})
variable ynew equal y[v_i]+v_deltamove*random(-1.0,1.0,${seed})
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L53-L54)

**Internal Variables** store fixed values for use with fixes and computes:

```
variable tcontrol internal 0.5
fix tstat all langevin v_tcontrol 0.5 0.5 2938940
```
Sources: [examples/controller/in.controller.temp](examples/controller/in.controller.temp#L19-L20)

## Variable Substitution Syntax

LAMMPS uses `${variable_name}` syntax for variable substitution. When LAMMPS encounters this pattern in an input script, it replaces it with the variable's current value before executing the command.

**Direct substitution** replaces variables with their literal values:

```
lattice hex ${density}
region box block 0 10 0 5 -0.5 0.5
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L13-L14)

**Chained substitutions** allow variables to reference other variables:

```
variable x atom x+v_deltaperturb*random(-1.0,1.0,${seed})
set group all x v_x
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L32-L33)

**Variable references in formulas** use the `$` prefix without braces for equal-style variables:

```
variable e equal pe
variable emin equal $e
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L26-L29)

## Mathematical Expressions and Functions

Variables can contain complex mathematical expressions and built-in functions for calculations.

**Random number generation** uses the `random(min, max, seed)` function:

```
variable rn equal random(0.0,1.0,${seed})
variable irandom equal floor(atoms*random(0.0,1.0,${seed})+1)
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L51-L52)

**Mathematical functions** include exponential, trigonometric, and other operations:

```
variable boltzfactor equal "exp(atoms*(v_elast - v_e) / v_kT)"
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L55)

**Atom property access** uses array indexing notation with `x[id]`, `y[id]`, `z[id]`:

```
variable xi equal x[v_i]
variable yi equal y[v_i]
variable xnew equal x[v_i]+v_deltamove*random(-1.0,1.0,${seed})
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L56-L58)

## Control Flow Structures

LAMMPS provides several constructs for controlling script execution flow, enabling loops, conditional logic, and jumps.

### Labels and Jumps

The `label` command marks a location in the script that can be jumped to, enabling loops:

```
label loop
# ... commands to be repeated ...
next iter
jump SELF loop
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L61-L107-L108)

The `next` command advances a loop variable, and `jump SELF label` creates an unconditional jump to the specified label, forming the basic structure of a loop.

### Conditional Execution

The `if` command provides conditional logic with optional `elif` and `else` clauses:

```
if "$e <= ${elast}" then &
  "variable elast equal $e" &
  "variable naccept equal ${increment}" &
elif "${rn} <= ${boltzfactor}" &
  "variable elast equal $e" &
  "variable naccept equal ${increment}" &
else &
  "set atom $i x ${x0}" &
  "set atom $i y ${y0}"
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L102-L108)

Conditional expressions can use comparison operators (`<=`, `>=`, `<`, `>`, `==`, `!=`) and logical operators to evaluate variable values or computed expressions.

## Variable Categories Summary

| Variable Type | Style Keyword | Purpose | Example Use Case |
|--------------|---------------|---------|------------------|
| Index | `index` | Single value from list | `variable temp index 300 400 500` |
| Equal | `equal` | Computed expression | `variable press equal press` |
| Loop | `loop` | Loop counter | `variable i loop 100` |
| Atom | `atom` | Per-atom calculations | `variable vx atom vx` |
| Internal | `internal` | Fixed value for fixes | `variable cv internal 0.5` |
| World | `world` | Partition-specific values | `variable seed world 123 456 789` |
| Universe | `universe` | Multiple independent runs | `variable T universe 200 300 400` |
| Uloop | `uloop` | Universe loop counter | `variable i uloop 100` |

## Practical Usage Patterns

### Monte Carlo Algorithm Implementation

The Monte Carlo example demonstrates advanced variable usage for implementing a Metropolis algorithm:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Define MC parameters] --> B[Run 0 steps for baseline energy]
    B --> C[Perturb system positions]
    C --> D[Calculate new energy]
    D --> E{Energy lower?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Accept move]
    E -->|No| G{Acceptance criteria?}
    G -->|Yes| F
    G -->|No| H[Reject move, restore positions]
    F --> I[Update acceptance statistics]
    H --> I
    I --> J{Loop complete?}
    J -->|No| K[Select random atom]
    K --> L[Propose new position]
    L --> D
    J -->|Yes| M[Output final statistics]
```

Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L2-L108)

> [!TIP]
> Loop variables must be paired with `next` commands to advance iteration, and `jump SELF label` to create the actual loop structure. Without both components, the loop will not execute correctly.

### Dynamic Load Balancing with Variables

Variables enable adaptive load balancing during simulation by tracking and updating processor weights:

```
fix 0 all balance 50 1.0 shift x 10 1.0 &
  weight var lastweight weight time 0.5 weight store WEIGHT
variable maximb equal f_0[1]
variable iter equal f_0[2]
```
Sources: [examples/balance/in.balance.var.dynamic](examples/balance/in.balance.var.dynamic#L27-L30)

### Atom-Level Property Manipulation

Variables can manipulate individual atom properties for complex algorithmic operations:

```
variable xnew equal x[v_i]+v_deltamove*random(-1.0,1.0,${seed})
set atom $i x ${xnew}
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L53-L68)

> [!TIP]
> When using atom variables in `set` commands, ensure the atom ID exists. Out-of-range atom IDs will cause errors, so validate atom counts before accessing specific atoms.

## Integration with LAMMPS Commands

Variables integrate seamlessly with LAMMPS commands across multiple categories:

**Fix commands** can use variable parameters for adaptive control:
```
fix tstat all langevin v_tcontrol 0.5 0.5 2938940
```
Sources: [examples/controller/in.controller.temp](examples/controller/in.controller.temp#L20)

**Set commands** apply variable values to atoms and groups:
```
set atom $i x ${xnew}
set group all x v_x
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L68-L33)

**Compute commands** create new variables from simulation properties:
```
variable e equal pe
compute p all property/atom d_WEIGHT
```
Sources: [examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc](examples/MC-LOOP/in.mc#L25-L28), [examples/balance/in.balance.var.dynamic](examples/balance/in.balance.var.dynamic#L16-L17)

## Best Practices

1. **Use descriptive variable names** that clearly indicate their purpose and type
2. **Initialize variables early** in the script before they're referenced
3. **Test conditional logic** with simple cases before complex algorithms
4. **Validate loop bounds** to prevent infinite loops in `jump` constructs
5. **Document variable units** and expected value ranges in comments
6. **Use internal variables** for fix parameters that should remain constant
7. **Leverage atom variables** for per-atom calculations rather than multiple compute commands

## Common Variable Operations

| Operation | Syntax | Example |
|-----------|--------|---------|
| Define variable | `variable name style value` | `variable T equal 300` |
| Reference variable | `${name}` or `$name` | `region box 0 ${L} 0 ${L}` |
| Compute expression | `math functions` | `variable e equal pe+ke` |
| Access atom property | `property[id]` | `variable xi equal x[v_i]` |
| Generate random | `random(min,max,seed)` | `variable rn equal random(0,1,12345)` |
| Increment loop variable | `next varname` | `next iter` |

## Next Steps

With variables and control flow mastered, explore how these concepts integrate with other LAMMPS features:

- **Reading and Writing Data Files** - Learn how variables can parameterize data file operations [Reading and Writing Data Files](14-reading-and-writing-data-files)
- **Advanced Scripting Techniques** - Discover sophisticated scripting patterns combining multiple control structures [Advanced Scripting Techniques](15-advanced-scripting-techniques)
- **Energy Minimization Algorithms** - See how variables control optimization parameters [Energy Minimization Algorithms](20-energy-minimization-algorithms)
- **Python Integration** - Learn about interfacing variables with Python workflows [LAMMPS Python Module Basics](28-lammps-python-module-basics)

Variables and control flow form the foundation of flexible, reusable LAMMPS scripts. Mastering these concepts enables you to create simulation workflows that adapt to different conditions, parameter studies, and complex algorithmic requirements.

# Reading and Writing Data Files



This page covers the essential aspects of data file management in LAMMPS, focusing on the structure of LAMMPS data files, how to read and write them programmatically, and the available conversion tools for interoperability with other molecular dynamics packages. Data files serve as the primary mechanism for initializing complex molecular systems, storing atom positions, topology information, and interaction parameters that define your simulation model.

## Data File Architecture

The LAMMPS data file format follows a structured, section-based organization that encodes all essential system information in a human-readable ASCII format. Each data file begins with a descriptive header containing global system counts, followed by sequential sections defining box geometry, atomic properties, interaction coefficients, and topological connectivity.

![LAMMPS Data File Structure](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/examples/peptide/data.peptide?raw=true)

```mermaid
graph TD
    A[Data File] --> B[Header Section]
    A --> C[Box Dimensions]
    A --> D[Masses Section]
    A --> E[Force Field Coefficients]
    A --> F[Topology Sections]
    A --> G[Atoms Section]
    
    B --> B1[Atom count]
    B --> B2[Bond/Angle/Dihedral counts]
    B --> B3[Type counts]
    
    C --> C1[xlo xhi]
    C --> C2[ylo yhi]
    C --> C3[zlo zhi]
    
    E --> E1[Pair Coeffs]
    E --> E2[Bond Coeffs]
    E --> E3[Angle Coeffs]
    E --> E4[Dihedral Coeffs]
    E --> E5[Improper Coeffs]
    
    F --> F1[Bonds]
    F --> F2[Angles]
    F --> F3[Dihedrals]
    F --> F4[Impropers]
    
    G --> G1[Atom ID]
    G --> G2[Molecule ID]
    G --> G3[Atom type]
    G --> G4[Charge]
    G --> G5[Coordinates]
    G --> G6[Image flags]
```

The header section establishes the system scope by declaring the total number of structural elements: atoms, bonds, angles, dihedrals, and impropers, along with the corresponding type counts for each category. This information enables LAMMPS to allocate appropriate memory structures and validate consistency across different sections [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L1-L15). Following the header, the box dimensions define the simulation cell boundaries using the standard LAMMPS convention with low and high bounds for each dimension [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L16-L18).

**Section Order Requirements**: The sequence of sections in a data file is significant and must follow a specific order to ensure proper parsing. While some sections are optional depending on the system complexity, their relative positioning cannot be arbitrarily rearranged. The masses section must precede the atoms section, and force field coefficient sections must appear before their corresponding topological sections. This ordering requirement reflects LAMMPS's sequential parsing algorithm which reads sections linearly and builds data structures progressively.

> [!TIP]
> When creating custom data files, ensure consistency between declared counts in the header and actual entries in each section. Mismatches between declared and actual bond counts are a common source of errors and can lead to undefined behavior or crashes during simulation initialization.

## Reading Data Files

Reading data files into LAMMPS is accomplished through the `read_data` command, which serves as the primary interface for loading pre-configured molecular systems. This command accepts the data file path and provides numerous optional flags for controlling which sections to read and how to handle various file format variations.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Input Script] --> B[read_data command]
    B --> C{Parse file sections}
    C --> D[Header validation]
    D --> E[Mass assignment]
    E --> F[Force field coefficients]
    F --> G[Topology connectivity]
    G --> H[Atom positions]
    H --> I[System initialization complete]
    
    C -->|Missing section| J[Skip/Use defaults]
    F -->|Style mismatch| K[Error/Fallback]
```

The basic syntax for reading a data file is straightforward: `read_data file.data`, but production scripts typically include additional parameters to handle specific simulation requirements. These parameters allow selective section reading, coordinate transformations, and compatibility with different data file versions [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L1-L6532). When reading molecular systems with bonded interactions, LAMMPS automatically establishes the topological connectivity defined in the bonds, angles, dihedrals, and impropers sections, enabling subsequent force computations.

**Section Selection**: The `read_data` command provides granular control over which sections to process through the `extra/...` keywords. For systems that don't require certain topological elements (such as dihedrals or impropers), you can selectively exclude these sections to reduce memory overhead and initialization time. Conversely, for specialized simulations requiring additional bond types or angle definitions, the `extra/bond/types`, `extra/angle/types`, and related keywords allow reading beyond what's initially declared in the header.

**Coordinate Transformations**: LAMMPS supports automatic coordinate transformations during data file loading through parameters like `shift`, `scale`, and `wrap`. These transformations enable seamless integration of data files generated with different coordinate conventions or unit systems without requiring manual pre-processing. The shift parameter applies a uniform translation to all coordinates, while scale applies multiplicative scaling factors to each dimension independently.

## Writing Data Files

Writing data files from within LAMMPS simulations enables checkpointing, analysis, and data exchange workflows. The `write_data` command creates complete data files representing the current system state, including all atom positions, velocities (when supported), topological information, and force field parameters.

**Complete System Dump**: When `write_data` is executed without specifying sections, LAMMPS generates a comprehensive data file containing all system information. This includes the header with current atom and topology counts, box dimensions reflecting any deformation or changes during simulation, masses, force field coefficients, complete topological connectivity, and atom positions. For molecular systems, the molecule IDs are preserved, enabling subsequent analysis of molecular integrity and connectivity [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L1-L6532).

**Selective Writing**: The `write_data` command supports selective section writing through the `pair`, `bond`, `angle`, `dihedral`, `improper` keywords. These boolean flags control whether force field coefficient sections are included in the output file. When working with fixed force fields that don't change between simulations, excluding coefficient sections can significantly reduce file sizes and prevent inadvertent parameter modifications.

**Velocity Output**: While standard data files don't include velocity information, the `write_data` command can optionally write velocities when the system has been initialized with velocities and the appropriate flag is set. This capability enables full state checkpointing for restart workflows, though for production restart scenarios, LAMMPS's native restart file format typically offers superior efficiency and completeness.

> [!TIP]
> For large molecular systems, consider writing data files at strategic simulation milestones rather than at regular intervals. The I/O overhead for writing complete data files scales with system size and can significantly impact simulation performance, especially on parallel file systems with limited bandwidth.

## Force Field Coefficients Format

The coefficient sections in LAMMPS data files define the parameters for various interaction types, with specific formatting requirements that depend on the chosen interaction style. Each coefficient type follows a consistent pattern: an integer type identifier followed by style-dependent parameter values.

**Pair Coefficients**: Pair coefficient sections define non-bonded interaction parameters between atom types. The exact format depends on the pair style specified in the input script. For Lennard-Jones style interactions, the typical format includes epsilon and sigma parameters, possibly with optional cutoff values [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L33-L46). More complex pair styles like EAM (Embedded Atom Method) require tabulated data or additional parameters for the embedding function and electron density contributions.

**Bond Coefficients**: Bond coefficients define parameters for covalent bond interactions, typically following the format `type K r0` where K represents the force constant and r0 is the equilibrium bond length for harmonic bond styles [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L47-L64). Different bond styles (Morse, FENE, quartic, etc.) require different parameter sets, and the data file format must match the expectations of the specified bond style in the input script.

**Angle, Dihedral, and Improper Coefficients**: These sections define parameters for bonded interactions involving three, four, and four atoms respectively. Angle coefficients typically include force constants and equilibrium angles [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L65-L95). Dihedral coefficients follow style-dependent formats, with harmonic styles requiring force constants, periodicity, phase shifts, and optionally multiplicity parameters [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L96-L116). Improper coefficients maintain planarity constraints in molecular systems and follow similar conventions [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L117-L120).

## Topology Sections

The topological sections (Atoms, Bonds, Angles, Dihedrals, Impropers) define the connectivity information that enables bonded force computations. Each entry follows a specific format that varies depending on the atom style and interaction type.

**Atoms Section**: The atoms section format depends on the specified atom style. For molecular systems with full atom information (typically `atom_style full`), each atom entry includes: atom ID, molecule ID, atom type, charge, and three coordinates [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L121-L200). For simpler atomic systems, the format may exclude molecule ID and charge fields. The image flags at the end of each line track which periodic images atoms belong to, enabling proper computation of periodic boundary conditions.

**Bonds, Angles, Dihedrals, Impropers**: These sections define the connectivity information for bonded interactions. Each entry typically includes: interaction ID, type identifier, and the list of atom indices participating in the interaction [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide#L121-L200). For bonds, this is two atom indices; for angles, three; for dihedrals and impropers, four. The interaction IDs are typically sequential but can be arbitrary as long as they're unique within each section.

## Conversion Tools

LAMMPS provides several utility scripts for converting between different molecular simulation file formats, facilitating interoperability with other packages and preprocessing workflows. These tools are located in the `tools/` directory and cover common molecular simulation formats.

**AMBER to LAMMPS**: The `amber2lmp/` directory contains Python scripts for converting AMBER coordinate and topology files to LAMMPS data file format [amber2lammps.py](tools/amber2lmp/amber2lammps.py#L1-L821). The primary script handles both `.crd` coordinate files and `.top` topology files, extracting molecular topology, atom types, charges, and force field parameters. Conversion includes proper handling of periodic boundary conditions, mass assignments, and parameter mapping between AMBER's force field conventions and LAMMPS's parameter formats [amber2lmp/README](tools/amber2lmp/README#L1-L104).

**CHARMM to LAMMPS**: The `ch2lmp/` directory provides Perl scripts for converting CHARMM coordinate and parameter files to LAMMPS format. These scripts handle CHARMM's parameter file format and map CHARMM atom types and force field parameters to LAMMPS conventions. The conversion supports CHARMM's comprehensive force field including bonded terms, non-bonded interactions, and special handling for CHARMM's specific conventions like 1-4 scaling factors [ch2lmp/README](tools/ch2lmp/README).

**TINKER to LAMMPS**: The `tinker/` directory contains Python scripts for converting TINKER XYZ and parameter files to LAMMPS format. This conversion is particularly useful for accessing TINKER's extensive parameter library and its support for polarizable force fields. The scripts handle TINKER's coordinate conventions and parameter file formats [tinker/data.py](tools/tinker/data.py).

| Conversion Tool | Source Format | Target Format | Language |
|----------------|---------------|---------------|----------|
| amber2lammps | AMBER .crd/.top | LAMMPS data | Python |
| charmm2lammps | CHARMM .psf/.prm | LAMMPS data | Perl |
| tinker2lmp | TINKER .xyz/.prm | LAMMPS data | Python |
| lmp2cfg | LAMMPS dump | CFG format | Fortran |
| dump2xyz | LAMMPS dump | XYZ format | Python |

**Utility Scripts**: Beyond format conversion, the `tools/` directory contains numerous utility scripts for data manipulation and analysis. The `lmp2cfg/` tool converts LAMMPS dump files to CFG format for visualization in Atomeye [lmp2cfg/lmp2cfg.f](tools/lmp2cfg/lmp2cfg.f). Python scripts in `tools/python/` provide dump file conversion to various formats including PDB and XYZ, plus utilities for sorting and analyzing dump files [tools/python/dump2xyz.py](tools/python/dump2xyz.py), [tools/python/dump2pdb.py](tools/python/dump2pdb.py).

> [!TIP]
> When using conversion tools, always validate the converted system by checking mass sums, charge neutrality, and bond connectivity before proceeding with production simulations. Conversion scripts may occasionally fail to map complex force field features, particularly for specialized atom types or non-standard interaction parameters.

## Best Practices and Common Patterns

**File Organization**: Organize data files with descriptive naming conventions that indicate system type, force field, and creation date. For molecular systems, include information about the molecular composition in the filename or a separate README file. Maintain separate directories for different molecular systems or force field variants to avoid confusion between similar data files.

**Validation Workflow**: Establish a systematic validation workflow when creating or modifying data files. Begin by verifying that section counts match actual entries, check that all atom types have corresponding mass definitions, ensure charge neutrality (for systems requiring electrostatic calculations), and validate that all bonded interactions reference valid atom IDs. Many validation steps can be automated through simple Python scripts that parse the data file format and check consistency conditions.

**Incremental Building**: For complex molecular systems, consider building data files incrementally using a hierarchy of smaller, validated components. Start with basic atomic positions, add molecular topology gradually, and incorporate force field parameters systematically. This approach isolates errors to specific stages and makes debugging significantly easier than attempting to create complete data files in a single step.

**Version Control**: Track data files in version control systems alongside input scripts and analysis tools. While binary restart files are typically too large for efficient version control, data files for initialization are often of manageable size and benefit from tracking to maintain reproducibility. Document any modifications to data files in commit messages, including the rationale for parameter changes.

## Integration with Simulation Workflows

Data files serve as the bridge between system preparation, simulation execution, and analysis phases of molecular dynamics workflows. Understanding their role in each phase enables efficient workflow design and reproducible research practices.

**System Preparation**: Data files are typically the output of system preparation workflows that may involve molecular building tools, conversion utilities, or custom preprocessing scripts. The preparation phase focuses on generating physically reasonable initial configurations with appropriate topology and force field parameters. For complex molecular systems, tools like moltemplate (available in `tools/moltemplate/`) provide templating systems for generating data files with molecular hierarchies [moltemplate/README.txt](tools/moltemplate/README.txt).

**Simulation Execution**: During simulation execution, data files are loaded once at initialization through the `read_data` command. The information contained in data files establishes the complete system state before simulation begins, including positions, connectivity, and interaction parameters. Subsequent modifications to the system (such as adding or deleting atoms, changing interactions, or applying deformations) typically occur through LAMMPS commands rather than data file manipulation.

**Analysis and Restart**: Data files written during or after simulation provide snapshots for analysis and can serve as starting points for subsequent simulations. For analysis workflows, data files enable extraction of topological information, connectivity analysis, and force field parameter inspection. For restart workflows, while LAMMPS restart files provide more complete state information, data files can serve as simplified restart points when only atomic positions and topology are needed.

## Advanced Data File Features

**Triclinic Systems**: LAMMPS data files support triclinic simulation boxes through the inclusion of three tilt factors (xy, xz, yz) following the box dimension specifications. These tilt factors define the off-diagonal elements of the box matrix and enable simulation of systems with non-orthogonal periodic boundaries. The conversion between triclinic and orthogonal representations requires careful attention to coordinate transformations.

**Multiple Time Step Parameters**: Some advanced force field implementations require multiple parameter sets for different interaction cutoffs or time step schemes. Data files can accommodate these requirements through multiple coefficient sections or specialized formatting conventions. When using such advanced features, consult the specific documentation for the relevant pair, bond, or angle styles to understand the expected data file format.

**Molecule Templates**: For systems with repeated molecular units, data files can be combined with molecule templates defined through the `molecule` command. This approach enables efficient specification of complex molecular topologies by defining molecules once and instantiating them multiple times with different positions and orientations. While molecule templates are typically defined in separate molecule files rather than data files, understanding their integration with data files is important for advanced molecular system construction.

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

**Missing or Extra Atoms**: Errors indicating mismatched atom counts typically result from discrepancies between the header declaration and actual atom entries. Verify that the atom count in the header matches the number of lines in the Atoms section, and check for blank lines or commented entries that might confuse the parser. For systems created programmatically, ensure that atom ID assignment is contiguous starting from 1.

**Undefined Atom Types**: When LAMMPS encounters atom types without corresponding mass definitions or force field coefficients, it will generate errors during initialization. Verify that all atom types appearing in the Atoms section have entries in the Masses section, and that all referenced types in bonded interactions have corresponding coefficient definitions. Pay particular attention to off-by-one errors in type numbering.

**Bond Connectivity Errors**: Errors in bond, angle, dihedral, or improper sections often reference atoms that don't exist or fall outside valid ID ranges. Check that all atom indices in topological sections correspond to valid atom IDs from the Atoms section. For molecules, verify that the molecule IDs are consistent and that bonded interactions don't cross molecule boundaries unless intentionally designed.

**Force Field Parameter Mismatches**: When using converted data files, ensure that the force field parameters in the coefficient sections are appropriate for the specified pair, bond, and angle styles in the input script. Different packages may use different parameter conventions (epsilon/sigma vs. A/B for Lennard-Jones, for example), and conversion scripts must map these correctly. Test simple systems with known properties to validate parameter assignments.

For further guidance on LAMMPS commands and simulation techniques, continue with [Advanced Scripting Techniques](15-advanced-scripting-techniques) or explore [Dump Files and Trajectory Output](32-dump-files-and-trajectory-output) for alternative data storage and visualization options.

# Advanced Scripting Techniques



This page explores sophisticated scripting capabilities that extend beyond basic LAMMPS input scripts. These techniques enable complex simulation protocols, Python-LAMMPS integration, and advanced workflow orchestration for researchers pushing the boundaries of molecular dynamics simulations.

## Variable Reference Systems

LAMMPS provides a powerful variable expansion system that allows dynamic parameter substitution and runtime configuration. The variable system supports multiple types with distinct behaviors and use cases.

### Variable Types and Syntax

The variable system in LAMMPS enables script parameterization and mathematical operations through several categories:

```lammps
# Index variables - defined in scripts, expandable at command line
variable mu index -1.25
variable temp index 2.0
variable disp index 1.0
variable lbox index 5.0

# Equal variables - compute thermodynamic quantities
variable rho equal density
variable p equal press
variable muex equal ${mu}-${temp}*ln(density*${lambda}+${nugget})

# Atom variables - per-atom properties
variable fx atom fx
variable vy atom vy
```

Sources: [examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj](examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj#L8-L10), [examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj](examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj#L29-L31), [python/examples/in.simple](python/examples/in.simple#L23)

> [!TIP]
> Variables can be overridden from the command line using `-var name value` switches, enabling flexible parameter sweeps without script modification. This is particularly useful for high-throughput simulations and optimization workflows.

### Dynamic Group Composition

Advanced scripts leverage dynamic groups that update based on variable conditions:

```lammps
# Dynamic group based on atom property
variable type1 atom "type==1"
group type1 dynamic gcmcgroup var type1
variable n1 equal count(type1)
```

Sources: [examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj](examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj#L22-L24)

This pattern enables real-time tracking of particle populations during grand canonical Monte Carlo simulations, where atom counts fluctuate dynamically.

## Python-LAMMPS Integration

The Python module provides programmatic control over LAMMPS, enabling hybrid workflows that combine LAMMPS simulation power with Python's scientific ecosystem.

### Core Integration Patterns

Python scripts can execute LAMMPS commands, extract simulation data, modify atomic configurations, and run simulations iteratively:

```python
# Initialize LAMMPS instance
lmp = lammps()

# Execute commands
lmp.command("run 10")

# Extract per-atom data
x = lmp.gather_atoms("x", 1, 3)
v = lmp.gather_atoms("v", 1, 3)

# Modify positions programmatically
epsilon = 0.1
x[0] += epsilon
lmp.scatter_atoms("x", 1, 3, x)

# Continue simulation
lmp.command("run 1")
```

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L35-L54)

### Data Extraction and Manipulation

The Python API offers multiple methods for accessing LAMMPS data, each optimized for different use cases:

| Method | Use Case | Performance Characteristics |
|--------|----------|----------------------------|
| `gather_atoms()` | Extract all atoms of a property | High overhead for large systems |
| `gather_atoms_concat()` | Concatenated global array | More memory efficient |
| `gather_atoms_subset()` | Specific atom IDs | Best for sparse access |

```python
# Full array extraction
x = lmp.gather_atoms("x", 1, 3)
f = lmp.gather_atoms("f", 1, 3)

# Subset extraction (IDs 2 and 4)
ids = (2*ctypes.c_int)()
ids[0] = 2
ids[1] = 4
x_subset = lmp.gather_atoms_subset("x", 1, 3, 2, ids)
f_subset = lmp.gather_atoms_subset("f", 1, 3, 2, ids)

# Selective updates
lmp.scatter_atoms_subset("x", 1, 3, 2, ids, x)
```

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L94-L116)

### Command Batching

Multiple command submission strategies optimize different workflow patterns:

```python
# String-based batch (multi-line)
strtwo = "run 10\nrun 20"
lmp.commands_string(strtwo)

# List-based batch
cmds = ["run 10", "run 20"]
lmp.commands_list(cmds)
```

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L66-L70)

> [!TIP]
> List-based batching through `commands_list()` is generally more efficient for generating commands programmatically, as it avoids string concatenation overhead and provides better error handling.

### Advanced Python Features

The Python wrapper enables complex simulation control including atom creation, box manipulation, and compute management:

```python
# Extract and modify simulation box
boxlo, boxhi, xy, yz, xz, periodicity, box_change = lmp.extract_box()
print("Box info", boxlo, boxhi, xy, yz, xz, periodicity, box_change)

# Reset box dimensions
lmp.reset_box([0, 0, 0], [10, 10, 8], 0, 0, 0)

# Create new atoms programmatically
natoms = lmp.get_natoms()
atype = natoms * [1]
lmp.create_atoms(natoms, None, atype, x, v)
```

Sources: [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L76-L81), [python/examples/simple.py](python/examples/simple.py#L122-L128)

## Multi-System and Hybrid Atom Styles

Advanced simulations often require combining multiple atom types or simulation styles within a single run. LAMMPS supports hybrid and template atom styles for these scenarios.

### Template Atom Style

The template atom style enables molecular template definitions with parameterized insertion:

```lammps
# Define molecular template
molecule cychex cyclohexane.mol
atom_style template cychex

# Create system with template molecules
lattice sc 6.0
variable boxlen index 4.0
region box block -${boxlen} ${boxlen} -${boxlen} ${boxlen} -${boxlen} ${boxlen} units lattice
create_box 2 box bond/types 1 angle/types 1 dihedral/types 1

# Insert template molecules randomly
create_atoms 0 box mol cychex 734594

# Add other atom types
create_atoms 2 random 800 495437 box
```

Sources: [examples/template/in.template-mix](examples/template/in.template-mix#L4-L17)

### Hybrid Atom Styles

The hybrid atom style enables combining multiple atom representations:

```lammps
# Define multiple molecular templates
molecule twomols h2o.mol co2.mol offset 2 1 1 0 0

# Combine template and charge styles
atom_style hybrid template twomols charge
```

Sources: [examples/template/in.hybrid](examples/template/in.hybrid#L3-L5)

This architecture allows simulating complex mixtures where different molecules require different internal representations, such as combining rigid water molecules with flexible CO₂ molecules in a single simulation.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Molecule Definitions"] --> B["Template Database"]
    B --> C["Hybrid Atom Style"]
    C --> D["Template Substyle"]
    C --> E["Charge Substyle"]
    D --> F["Rigid Water"]
    D --> G["Flexible CO2"]
    E --> H["Electrostatics"]
    
    style C fill:#e1f5ff
    style D fill:#fff4e1
    style E fill:#fff4e1
```

## Multi-Neighbor List Optimization

For systems with widely varying particle sizes or interaction radii, multi-neighbor lists provide significant performance improvements.

### Configuration Pattern

```lammps
# Configure multi-level neighbor lists
neighbor 1 multi
neigh_modify delay 0 collection/type 2 1*4 5
comm_modify mode multi reduce/multi
```

Sources: [examples/multi/in.colloid](examples/multi/in.colloid#L23-L25), [examples/multi/in.powerlaw](examples/multi/in.powerlaw#L10-L12)

The `collection/type` syntax defines how to group atom types for neighbor list construction, while `collection/interval` groups by interaction distance.

| Parameter | Type | Description |
|-----------|------|-------------|
| `collection/type` | type-based | Groups atoms by type for separate neighbor lists |
| `collection/interval` | distance-based | Groups by interaction radius intervals |
| `reduce/multi` | communication optimization | Reduces communication overhead for heterogeneous systems |

### Granular Systems with Multi-Lists

Power-law distributed granular systems particularly benefit from multi-neighbor lists:

```lammps
# Power-law size distribution
neighbor 1 multi
neigh_modify delay 0 collection/interval 6 1.5 3 10 30 100 200
comm_modify mode multi vel yes reduce/multi

# Granular interactions
pair_style granular
pair_coeff * * hooke 20.0 0.5 tangential linear_history 1.0 0.5 0.1 damping mass_velocity
```

Sources: [examples/multi/in.powerlaw](examples/multi/in.powerlaw#L10-L13)

This configuration creates six separate neighbor list levels based on particle radii, optimizing for the extreme size variation in power-law distributions.

## Advanced Simulation Protocols

### Grand Canonical Monte Carlo Integration

GCMC simulations require careful scripting to balance molecular dynamics with Monte Carlo insertion/deletion moves:

```lammps
# Define tunable parameters
variable mu index -1.25
variable temp index 2.0
variable disp index 1.0

# GCMC fix with displacement moves
fix mygcmc gcmcgroup gcmc 1 100 100 1 29494 ${temp} ${mu} ${disp}

# Compute chemical potential
variable nugget equal 1.0e-8
variable lambda equal 1.0
variable muex equal ${mu}-${temp}*ln(density*${lambda}+${nugget})

# Track acceptance rates
variable tacc equal f_mygcmc[2]/(f_mygcmc[1]+${nugget})
variable iacc equal f_mygcmc[4]/(f_mygcmc[3]+${nugget})
variable dacc equal f_mygcmc[6]/(f_mygcmc[5]+${nugget})
```

Sources: [examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj](examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj#L8-L40)

The fix syntax `gcmc 1 100 100 1` defines move attempts (1 translation, 100 insertion, 100 deletion moves) per GCMC cycle.

### Widom Insertion Method

For chemical potential calculations without modifying the system composition:

```lammps
# Widom insertion test particles
fix mywidom all widom 10 100000 2 29494 0.75

# Track insertion statistics
thermo_style custom step temp pe etotal press vol density f_mywidom[1] f_mywidom[2] f_mywidom[3]
```

Sources: [examples/mc/in.widom.lj](examples/mc/in.widom.lj#L16-L18)

The Widom method provides accurate excess chemical potential estimates through ghost particle insertions, preserving system equilibrium.

## Granular Flow Simulation Patterns

Granular materials require specialized scripting for particle insertion and flow initialization.

### Pour Operations

The pour fix enables gradual particle insertion for realistic settling:

```lammps
# Define insertion region
region slab block -9.0 9.0 -9.0 9.0 10.0 15.0 units box

# Pour particles with controlled volume fraction
fix ins all pour 3000 1 300719 vol 0.13 50 region slab

# Two-stage simulation: settling then flow
run 25000
unfix ins
fix 2 all gravity 1.0 chute 26.0
run 25000
```

Sources: [examples/pour/in.pour](examples/pour/in.pour#L28-L52)

This pattern creates realistic initial conditions for granular flow simulations by allowing particles to settle under gravity before initiating flow by reorienting the gravity vector.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A["Define Container"] --> B["Set Gravity Vertical"]
    B --> C["Pour Particles<br>gradually"]
    C --> D["Settling Phase<br>run 25000"]
    D --> E["Reorient Gravity<br>chute 26.0"]
    E --> F["Flow Phase<br>run 25000"]
    
    style D fill:#e1f5ff
    style F fill:#fff4e1
```

## Performance Optimization Techniques

### Dynamic Group Management

Advanced scripts minimize computational overhead through selective group operations:

```lammps
# Dedicated group for expensive operations
group gcmcgroup type 1

# Apply fixes only to relevant atoms
fix mygcmc gcmcgroup gcmc 1 100 100 1 29494 ${temp} ${mu} ${disp}
```

Sources: [examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj](examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj#L19-L22)

This pattern is crucial for hybrid simulations where only a subset of atoms requires special treatment (e.g., GCMC moves on solvent while solute remains fixed).

### Thermodynamic Output Control

Custom thermo configurations extract precisely needed information:

```lammps
# Monitor acceptance rates and derived quantities
thermo_style custom step temp press pe ke density atoms v_iacc v_dacc v_tacc v_rhoav v_pav v_muexav v_n1av
thermo 1000

# Average over windows
fix ave all ave/time 10 100 1000 v_rho v_p v_muex v_n1 ave one file rho_vs_p.dat
variable rhoav equal f_ave[1]
variable pav equal f_ave[2]
```

Sources: [examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj](examples/mc/in.gcmc.lj#L33-L43)

The averaging fix reduces output volume while providing statistically meaningful quantities through sliding window analysis.
