# Pair Styles Overview



This page introduces LAMMPS pair styles—the fundamental mechanism for defining non-bonded interactions between atoms. Pair styles calculate forces and energies between pairs of atoms based on their interatomic distances, enabling simulation of materials from noble gases to complex biomolecules. Understanding pair styles is essential for accurate molecular dynamics simulations.

![LAMMPS Logo](https://github.com/lammps/lammps/blob/develop/doc/src/JPG/lammps-logo.jpg?raw=true)

Sources: [pair.h](src/pair.h#L1-L150), [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L1-L50)

## Pair Style Architecture

LAMMPS implements pair styles through an object-oriented hierarchy centered on the abstract `Pair` base class. Each concrete pair style inherits from this base class and implements virtual methods for force/energy computation, parameter management, and initialization. This design enables LAMMPS to support over 200 different pair styles while maintaining a consistent interface.

```mermaid
classDiagram
    class Pair {
        +double eng_vdwl
        +double eng_coul
        +double virial[6]
        +compute(int eflag, int vflag)*
        +settings(int narg, char** arg)*
        +coeff(int narg, char** arg)*
        +init_style()
        +init_one(int i, int j)*
        +single()*
    }
    
    class PairLJCut {
        +compute(int eflag, int vflag)
        +coeff(int narg, char** arg)
        +init_one(int i, int j)
        -double** epsilon
        -double** sigma
        -double** cut
    }
    
    class PairBuck {
        +compute(int eflag, int vflag)
        +coeff(int narg, char** arg)
        -double** A
        -double** rho
        -double** C
    }
    
    class PairHybrid {
        +compute(int eflag, int vflag)
        +coeff(int narg, char** arg)
        -Pair** styles
        -int nstyles
    }
    
    Pair <|-- PairLJCut
    Pair <|-- PairBuck
    Pair <|-- PairHybrid
```

The `Pair` base class stores fundamental properties including van der Waals energy (`eng_vdwl`), Coulomb energy (`eng_coul`), and the six-component virial tensor [pair.h](src/pair.h#L58-L64). Each derived class must override the pure virtual `compute()` method, which performs the actual force and energy calculations, along with `settings()` and `coeff()` methods for parameter setup.

Sources: [pair.h](src/pair.h#L56-L135), [pair_lj_cut.h](src/pair_lj_cut.h#L30-L64)

## Force Computation Mechanics

The core of every pair style is the `compute()` method, which loops over atom pairs within a specified cutoff distance and calculates forces based on the interaction potential. This method receives energy and virial flags that control whether these quantities are accumulated during computation.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[compute call] --> B[Initialize arrays]
    B --> C[Loop over local atoms]
    C --> D[Loop over neighbors]
    D --> E{rsq < cutoff?}
    E -->|Yes| F[Calculate force]
    E -->|No| J[Continue]
    F --> G[Update forces]
    G --> H{eflag set?}
    H -->|Yes| I[Calculate energy]
    H -->|No| J[Continue]
    I --> J
    J --> K{evflag set?}
    K -->|Yes| L[Call ev_tally]
    K -->|No| D
    L --> D
    C --> M[Finalize virial]
    M --> N[End]
```

In `PairLJCut`, the implementation demonstrates the typical pattern: iterate through the neighbor list, calculate the squared distance (`rsq`), and if within the cutoff, compute the Lennard-Jones force and energy [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L69-L143). The force is derived from the potential derivative and applied equally and oppositely to both atoms following Newton's third law.

Sources: [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L69-L143), [pair.h](src/pair.h#L155-L162)

## Parameter Management and Mixing

Pair style parameters are organized into type-dependent arrays that specify interactions between each combination of atom types. The `allocate()` method creates these arrays sized according to the number of atom types in the system [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L397-L422). For example, `PairLJCut` allocates arrays for `epsilon`, `sigma`, `cut` (cutoff distance), and precomputed coefficients (`lj1` through `lj4`) that accelerate force calculations.

> [!TIP]
> When setting coefficients for mixed atom types (i≠j), LAMMPS can automatically compute parameters using mixing rules if you don't explicitly specify them. The `init_one()` method checks for unset coefficients and applies the selected mixing rule (geometric, arithmetic, or sixthpower) to derive cross-type parameters from like-type values.

The `coeff()` method accepts flexible type specifications using wildcards, allowing you to set parameters for multiple type pairs with a single command. For instance, `* * 0.01 3.4` sets the same epsilon and sigma for all type combinations [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L442-L475).

Sources: [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L397-L475), [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L720-L740)

## Common Pair Style Categories

LAMMPS provides pair styles organized by physical model and computational method. Selecting the appropriate style depends on your material system and required accuracy.

| Category | Representative Styles | Physical Model | Typical Use Cases |
|----------|----------------------|----------------|------------------|
| Simple Two-Body | `lj/cut`, `lj/expand`, `buck` | Analytical potentials with cutoffs | Noble gases, simple fluids |
| Truncated Shifted | `lj/cut/coul/long`, `lj/smooth` | Potentials shifted to zero at cutoff | Electrostatic systems, smooth truncation |
| Tabulated | `table`, `table/rx` | User-provided interpolation tables | Custom potentials, complex interactions |
| Many-Body | `eam`, `tersoff`, `reaxff` | Bond-order dependent, reactive potentials | Metals, covalent materials |
| Polarizable | `lj/cut/thole/long`, `dpd` | Include induced dipoles or coarse-graining | Polymers, biomolecules |
| Long-Range | `coul/long`, `ewald/n` | Coulomb interactions with Ewald/PPPM | Ionic systems, aqueous solutions |
| Hybrid | `hybrid`, `hybrid/scaled` | Combine multiple pair styles | Mixed materials, multi-physics |

The `PairLJCut` style implements the classic Lennard-Jones 12-6 potential with a simple radial cutoff. It's computationally efficient and suitable for noble gases and simple organic molecules. For metals requiring many-body effects, `eam` (Embedded Atom Method) captures the dependence of bond strength on local atomic coordination.

Sources: [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L1-L2032), [pair_lj_cut.h](src/pair_lj_cut.h#L1-L64)

## Hybrid Pair Styles

When simulating systems requiring multiple interaction types simultaneously, `pair_style hybrid` combines two or more pair styles, each applied to specific atom type pairs. This enables, for example, modeling a metal-polymer interface with EAM for metal atoms and Lennard-Jones for polymer interactions [pair_hybrid.cpp](src/pair_hybrid.cpp#L37-L1194).

The hybrid style manages an array of sub-styles, delegating compute calls to each relevant sub-style based on type mappings. Its `init_one()` method returns the maximum cutoff among all sub-styles to ensure neighbor lists encompass all interactions.

Sources: [pair_hybrid.cpp](src/pair_hybrid.cpp#L91-L98), [pair_hybrid.cpp](src/pair_hybrid.cpp#L714-L780)

## Energy and Virial Accounting

LAMMPS provides mechanisms for accurate energy and virial (stress tensor) computation through the `ev_tally()` family of methods. These methods accumulate contributions on a per-atom or global basis depending on compute flags [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L1030-L1182).

The `ev_tally()` method handles the most common case of two-body interactions, adding the pair's energy contribution to both atoms and computing the virial from the force components and separation vector. This ensures thermodynamic quantities like pressure are computed correctly regardless of the specific pair style implementation.

> [!TIP]
> Enable virial computation by setting the appropriate flags in your input script (`compute_style pressure all pressure` or `thermo_style custom pressure`). The virial is accumulated during force calculation only when requested, avoiding unnecessary computation overhead.

Sources: [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L911-L1010), [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L1030-L1132)

## Performance Optimization Features

LAMMPS includes several mechanisms to optimize pair style performance. Many pair styles support r-RESPA (multiple time step integration) through separate `compute_inner()`, `compute_middle()`, and `compute_outer()` methods that handle interactions at different distance ranges with different time steps [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L143-L298).

The base class provides table-based computation for long-range Coulomb interactions, storing precomputed values to avoid expensive transcendental function calls. The `init_tables()` method builds these interpolation tables based on the Coulomb cutoff and accuracy requirements [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L372-L686).

Modern LAMMPS also supports acceleration packages including GPU, Kokkos, and Intel variants of pair styles. These maintain the same interface but leverage hardware acceleration through specialized implementations (e.g., `pair_style lj/cut/gpu` or `pair_style lj/cut/kk`).

Sources: [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L143-L298), [pair.cpp](src/pair.cpp#L372-L686)

## Using Pair Styles in Input Scripts

Pair styles are specified in LAMMPS input scripts using the `pair_style` and `pair_coeff` commands. The style command selects the potential and its global parameters:

```text
pair_style lj/cut 10.0
pair_coeff * * 0.01 3.4 10.0
```

This selects the Lennard-Jones style with a 10.0 Å global cutoff and applies epsilon=0.01, sigma=3.4 Å to all type pairs. The `pair_coeff` command follows with type specifications and parameters specific to the chosen style.

For more complex systems requiring multiple interaction types, use hybrid styles:

```text
pair_style hybrid/overlay lj/cut 10.0 eam
pair_coeff * * lj/cut 0.01 3.4 10.0
pair_coeff * * eam Cu.eam
```

This combines Lennard-Jones and EAM potentials, with both contributing to the total interaction energy.

Sources: [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L422-L441), [pair_hybrid.cpp](src/pair_hybrid.cpp#L273-L393)

## Key Implementation Methods for Developers

For developers creating custom pair styles, several methods form the essential implementation contract:

| Method | Purpose | Required Override |
|--------|---------|-------------------|
| `compute(int eflag, int vflag)` | Calculate forces and energies | Yes (pure virtual) |
| `settings(int narg, char** arg)` | Parse global style parameters | Yes (pure virtual) |
| `coeff(int narg, char** arg)` | Parse type-specific parameters | Yes (pure virtual) |
| `allocate()` | Allocate parameter arrays | Usually |
| `init_style()` | Request neighbor lists, set options | Often |
| `init_one(int i, int j)` | Initialize parameters for type pair | Often |
| `single()` | Compute single pair interaction | Optional |
| `write_data()` / `read_restart()` | I/O operations | Optional |

The `PairLJCut` implementation provides a clear template for creating new pair styles, demonstrating proper allocation, coefficient parsing, mixing rule application, and force computation patterns [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L1-L705).

Sources: [pair.h](src/pair.h#L155-L220), [pair_lj_cut.cpp](src/pair_lj_cut.cpp#L1-L705)

## Next Steps

Pair styles are one component of LAMMPS's comprehensive force field system. To build complete models, you'll typically combine them with other interaction types:

- For bonded interactions (bonds, angles, dihedrals), see [Bond, Angle, and Dihedral Interactions](17-bond-angle-and-dihedral-interactions)
- For materials requiring reactive or many-body effects, explore [Many-Body and Reactive Potentials](18-many-body-and-reactive-potentials)
- For ionic or polar systems with long-range electrostatics, read about [Long-Range Electrostatics and K-space Methods](19-long-range-electrostatics-and-k-space-methods)

Understanding pair styles provides the foundation for accurately modeling non-bonded interactions, which combined with the other interaction types, enables realistic simulation of virtually any material system.


# Bond, Angle, and Dihedral Interactions



Bond, angle, and dihedral interactions form the foundation of molecular mechanics simulations in LAMMPS, enabling accurate modeling of covalent bonded systems including polymers, proteins, and small molecules. These interactions calculate forces arising from the stretching of chemical bonds, bending of bond angles, and rotation around dihedral angles. Unlike pair-wise interactions that operate between all atoms based on distance criteria, bonded interactions are topology-based—applied only to atoms explicitly connected in the molecular structure. This approach dramatically reduces computational cost while preserving chemical accuracy for systems where covalent bonding dominates the energy landscape.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L6-L9), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L7-L10)

## The Molecular Topology Architecture

Bonded interactions require a molecular topology definition that explicitly connects atoms through bonds, angles, and dihedrals. This topology is typically read from data files that list all bonded interactions along with their corresponding force field parameters. The topology information tells LAMMPS which atoms interact through bonded potentials, separating these specific interactions from the general non-bonded pair interactions. This architectural choice is fundamental to molecular mechanics simulation efficiency, as bonded interactions are O(N) in complexity rather than O(N²) for general pair interactions.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Molecular Structure] --> B[Data File Input]
    B --> C[Bonded Interactions]
    B --> D[Non-Bonded Interactions]
    C --> E[Bond Styles]
    C --> F[Angle Styles]
    C --> G[Dihedral Styles]
    C --> H[Improper Styles]
    D --> I[Pair Styles]
    C --> J[Force Calculation]
    I --> J
    J --> K[Integration]
```

The data file contains sections for each type of bonded interaction, specifying the atoms involved and parameters for the chosen potential style. For example, the peptide example demonstrates a complete molecular setup with multiple bond types using the CHARMM force field parameters.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L14), [data.peptide](examples/peptide/data.peptide)

## Bond Interaction Styles

Bond styles calculate the potential energy and forces associated with stretching chemical bonds between pairs of directly connected atoms. LAMMPS provides numerous bond styles optimized for different force fields and application scenarios. The **harmonic** bond style represents the most fundamental implementation, modeling bonds as harmonic springs with potential energy E = K(r - r₀)² where K is the force constant and r₀ is the equilibrium bond length. This style is widely used in classical force fields including CHARMM, AMBER, and DREIDING, providing computational efficiency and reasonable accuracy for small to moderate bond deformations.

| Bond Style | Force Field | Equation Type | Typical Applications |
|------------|-------------|---------------|---------------------|
| harmonic | CHARMM, AMBER, DREIDING | E = K(r - r₀)² | General organic molecules |
| fene | Polymer models | FENE potential | Coarse-grained polymers |
| morse | Reactive potentials | E = D[1-exp(-a(r-r₀))]² | Metal bonding, dissociation |
| class2 | COMPASS | Polynomial series | Polymers, materials |

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L6), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L8), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L7)

The harmonic bond style appears consistently across multiple examples, demonstrating its versatility. In the peptide simulation, harmonic bonds model the backbone and side-chain connectivity of a solvated peptide. The Dreiding example uses harmonic bonds for a methanol box system, showing applicability across different molecular types. The key advantage of harmonic bonds is their computational efficiency and well-understood parameterization, making them the default choice for most molecular mechanics simulations.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L6), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L8)

> [!TIP]
> When setting up harmonic bonds, ensure force constants and equilibrium lengths are consistent with the chosen force field. Parameter mixing between different force fields can lead to unphysical behavior. Always verify that bond parameters match the atom types defined in your pair style parameters.

## Angle Interaction Styles

Angle styles calculate forces arising from bond angle deformations, involving triplets of connected atoms where the middle atom is the vertex. The potential energy penalizes deviation from preferred equilibrium angles. Like bonds, angles are essential for maintaining molecular geometry and determining conformational flexibility. The **harmonic** angle style uses E = K(θ - θ₀)², while the **CHARMM** angle style adds cross-terms with Urey-Bradley corrections for improved accuracy in protein and nucleic acid simulations.

| Angle Style | Force Field | Key Features | Typical Applications |
|------------|-------------|--------------|---------------------|
| harmonic | General | Simple harmonic | Most organic molecules |
| charmm | CHARMM | Urey-Bradley terms | Proteins, nucleic acids |
| cosine | DREIDING | Cosine-based | Generic organic systems |
| class2 | COMPASS | Cross-coupling terms | Materials, polymers |

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L7), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L9), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L8)

The peptide example demonstrates the CHARMM angle style, which is particularly well-suited for biomolecular simulations. This style includes additional terms that couple angle bending with bond stretching (Urey-Bradley terms), capturing correlated motions important for protein dynamics. In contrast, the Dreiding example uses the harmonic angle style, which is more general purpose and computationally simpler. The choice between styles depends on the required accuracy and the force field being implemented.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L7), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L9)

## Dihedral and Torsional Potentials

Dihedral styles model rotations around central bonds, involving quartets of atoms and determining the energy barriers between different conformations. These interactions are crucial for describing stereochemistry, conformational preferences, and rotational dynamics. The complexity of dihedral potentials reflects the rich conformational landscape of organic molecules, where rotation around single bonds can create multiple energy minima corresponding to different staggered conformations.

LAMMPS implements several sophisticated dihedral styles:

- **charmm**: Fourier series with Urey-Bradley cross-terms, optimized for biomolecular force fields
- **harmonic**: Simple harmonic approximation around equilibrium dihedral angle
- **charmmfsw**: CHARMM force switch variant with modified switching functions
- **opls**: Optimized potentials for liquid simulations

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L8), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L9)

The CMAP example showcases the advanced **charmmfsw** dihedral style, which incorporates force switch functions for smooth energy transitions at interaction cutoffs. This is particularly important for maintaining energy conservation in molecular dynamics simulations of large biomolecules. The peptide example uses the standard CHARMM dihedral style, demonstrating the default approach for protein simulations. These dihedral implementations calculate multiple Fourier terms to accurately reproduce the rotational barriers derived from quantum mechanical calculations or experimental data.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L8), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L9)

## CMAP Corrections and Advanced Dihedrals

The Correction Map (CMAP) potential represents an advanced dihedral correction method developed for the CHARMM force field to improve backbone conformational accuracy in proteins. CMAP adds a two-dimensional correction term that depends on both the φ (phi) and ψ (psi) backbone dihedral angles, capturing correlations between successive torsional rotations that traditional dihedral potentials cannot represent. This correction is essential for accurate protein folding simulations and reproducing experimental Ramachandran plots.

Sources: [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L11-L12), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L13)

The CMAP example demonstrates the implementation through a specialized fix command: `fix cmap all cmap charmm22.cmap` reads the correction map parameters from a dedicated file. The CMAP data file contains a grid of energy values across the φ-ψ space, interpolated during simulation to apply corrections based on instantaneous backbone dihedral values. This approach provides significantly improved accuracy for protein secondary structure prediction compared to traditional single-dihedral potentials alone.

Sources: [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L11-L12), [charmm22.cmap](examples/cmap/charmm22.cmap)

> [!TIP]
> CMAP corrections are computationally expensive compared to standard dihedrals. For large protein systems, consider using CMAP selectively on the most important backbone regions or test whether the accuracy improvement justifies the computational cost for your specific application.

## Improper Interactions

Improper dihedrals maintain planarity or chirality in molecular structures, applying out-of-plane bending forces to quartets of atoms that shouldn't all lie in the same plane. These interactions are essential for maintaining the geometry of aromatic rings, tetrahedral carbon centers, and other stereochemically constrained environments. Improper potentials are distinct from proper dihedrals: they define a preferred angle between a central atom and the plane formed by three other atoms, rather than a rotational barrier.

The peptide example uses `improper_style harmonic` to maintain planarity of peptide bonds and other constrained geometries. The Dreiding example sets `improper_style none`, indicating that improper terms are not needed for that particular force field application. The choice depends on the chemical system's requirements: biomolecular force fields typically require impropers to maintain proper chirality and planarity, while simpler coarse-grained models may omit them.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L9), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L10)

## Integration with Pair Interactions

Bonded and non-bonded interactions must work together coherently through proper settings of the `special_bonds` command, which modifies how pair forces are computed between atoms connected through bonds, angles, or dihedrals. This is crucial for avoiding double-counting of interactions and implementing force field-specific scaling factors. The CHARMM force field, for example, uses specific scaling factors for 1-2 (bonded), 1-3 (angle-connected), and 1-4 (dihedral-connected) atom pairs.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L27), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L16)

The peptide example uses the convenient `special_bonds charmm` shorthand, which automatically applies the standard CHARMM scaling factors. The CMAP example demonstrates this same approach, showing consistency across CHARMM-based simulations. These settings ensure that electrostatic and van der Waals interactions between bonded atoms are properly scaled according to the force field's parameterization, preventing overcounting that would arise from applying both bonded and non-bonded potentials to the same atom pairs.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L27), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L16)

## Thermostat Integration with Constraint Algorithms

Bonded interactions often integrate with constraint algorithms like SHAKE, which freezes bond lengths to allow larger timesteps in molecular dynamics simulations. The peptide example demonstrates this with: `fix 2 all shake 0.0001 10 100 b 4 6 8 10 12 14 18 a 31`. This command constrains bonds with types 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14, 18 and angle type 31, effectively treating these bonds as rigid during integration.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L27)

SHAKE is particularly valuable for hydrogen-containing systems where fast X-H bond vibrations would otherwise force very small timesteps (on the order of 0.5 fs). By constraining these bonds, LAMMPS can use larger timesteps (typically 2.0 fs as shown in the examples) while maintaining numerical stability. The trade-off is that constrained bonds cannot participate in bond stretching energy calculations, which is acceptable for hydrogen bonds where the stretching dynamics are not of primary interest.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L26), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L35)

## Three-Body Potentials and Beyond

While this page focuses on bonded interactions, it's worth noting that LAMMPS also supports three-body potentials that can serve similar purposes in specialized systems. The **Stillinger-Weber** potential, demonstrated in the threebody example, explicitly includes three-body angular terms for silicon and other semiconductors. Similarly, **Tersoff** and **Vashishta** potentials include angular dependencies that conceptually resemble angle interactions, though they're implemented through pair styles rather than dedicated angle styles.

Sources: [in.threebody](examples/threebody/in.threebody#L50), [in.threebody](examples/threebody/in.threebody#L76)

These many-body potentials are essential for accurately modeling covalent materials where bond directionality and local coordination geometry determine properties. Unlike molecular force fields with explicit bond topology, many-body potentials determine bonding implicitly based on atomic distances and local coordination, making them suitable for modeling bond-breaking and formation events during reactive simulations.

Sources: [in.threebody](examples/threebody/in.threebody#L50), [in.threebody](examples/threebody/in.threebody#L83)

## Implementation Workflow

Setting up bonded interactions in LAMMPS follows a systematic workflow that ensures all components are properly configured:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Define Bond Style] --> B[Define Angle Style]
    B --> C[Define Dihedral Style]
    C --> D[Define Improper Style]
    D --> E[Configure Special Bonds]
    E --> F[Read Data File]
    F --> G[Set Pair Styles]
    G --> H[Configure Thermostat]
    H --> I[Run Simulation]
```

This workflow, demonstrated across all examples, ensures that bonded interactions are properly integrated with the rest of the simulation setup. The data file must contain sections matching the defined styles (Bonds, Angles, Dihedrals, Impropers) with parameters consistent with the chosen force field. The CMAP example shows an additional step where the CMAP fix must be specified before reading the data file so that the crossterm section can be properly processed.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L6-L14), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L7-L16)

## Energy Monitoring and Analysis

LAMMPS provides detailed energy output for bonded interactions through thermo output customization. All examples demonstrate thermo styles that include bonded energy terms (`ebond`, `eangle`, `edihed`, `eimp`) alongside kinetic, potential, and other energy components. This detailed output allows users to monitor the contribution of each bonded interaction type to the total energy, essential for debugging and validating simulation setups.

Sources: [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L30), [in.cmap](examples/cmap/in.cmap#L32)

The Dreiding example shows particularly comprehensive monitoring: `thermo_style custom etotal ke temp pe ebond eangle edihed eimp evdwl ecoul elong v_E_hbond v_C_hbond press vol` tracks all bonded energies plus hydrogen bond contributions, providing complete energy accounting for complex molecular systems. This level of detail is invaluable for understanding how different force components contribute to system behavior and for identifying potential problems in force field parameterization.

Sources: [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L30)

## Hybrid and Specialized Applications

LAMMPS supports advanced bonded interaction scenarios through hybrid styles and specialized fixes. The Dreiding example demonstrates `pair_style hybrid/overlay hbond/dreiding/lj 2 6 6.5 90 lj/cut/coul/long 8.5 11.5`, combining explicit hydrogen bonding potentials with standard Lennard-Jones and Coulomb interactions. This hybrid approach allows force field designers to implement complex interaction schemes that combine multiple physical effects.

Sources: [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L6)

The ability to layer different interaction types through hybrid styles provides flexibility for implementing custom force fields or studying systems where standard models are inadequate. Users should carefully consider the physical justification for each interaction component and ensure parameters are mutually consistent when building hybrid interaction schemes.

Sources: [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L6)

## Best Practices and Common Pitfalls

Successful implementation of bonded interactions requires attention to several critical details:

1. **Consistency**: Ensure all interaction styles (bond, angle, dihedral, improper, pair) belong to the same force field family. Mixing styles from different force fields can lead to unphysical behavior unless carefully validated.

2. **Parameter completeness**: Verify that all required parameters (force constants, equilibrium values, cross-terms) are provided in the data file for each bond, angle, and dihedral type. Missing or incorrect parameters are common sources of simulation failures.

3. **Special bonds**: Always set appropriate special bonds settings to avoid double-counting interactions. The `special_bonds charmm` command is frequently used but ensure it matches your force field's requirements.

4. **Timestep selection**: Choose timesteps appropriate for your system's fastest vibrational modes. Consider SHAKE or RATTLE constraints for hydrogen bonds to enable larger timesteps.

Sources: [in.peptide](examples/peptide/in.peptide#L6-L27), [in.dreiding](examples/dreiding/in.dreiding#L6-L16)

## Next Steps

After mastering basic bonded interactions, explore these advanced topics in the documentation catalog:

- [Pair Styles Overview](16-pair-styles-overview) to understand how bonded and non-bonded interactions work together
- [Many-Body and Reactive Potentials](18-many-body-and-reactive-potentials) for systems where bonds can break and form
- [Energy Minimization Algorithms](20-energy-minimization-algorithms) for optimizing molecular structures with bonded interactions
- [Reading and Writing Data Files](14-reading-and-writing-data-files) for creating custom molecular topologies

Bond, angle, and dihedral interactions provide the foundation for accurate molecular mechanics simulations. Through proper understanding and implementation of these interactions, you can model the rich conformational dynamics of molecular systems across chemistry, biology, and materials science.

# Many-Body and Reactive Potentials



Many-body and reactive potentials represent advanced interatomic interaction models that go beyond simple pairwise interactions. These potentials capture complex bonding behavior including bond-order effects, charge transfer, and chemical reactions, making them essential for simulating covalent materials, metallic systems, and chemical processes. Unlike simple pair potentials, these models incorporate many-body effects where the interaction between two atoms depends on the local atomic environment, enabling realistic description of bond breaking and formation, coordination-dependent bonding, and charge redistribution.

Sources: [potentials/README](potentials/README#L1-L20)

## Architectural Overview of Many-Body Potentials

LAMMPS implements a hierarchical architecture for many-body and reactive potentials that separates mathematical models from computational infrastructure. The architecture supports multiple potential families through unified interfaces while allowing optimization for specific physics models.

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Many-Body Potential Families"
        BP[Bond-Order Potentials<br/>Tersoff, AIREBO]
        EAM[Embedded Atom Methods<br/>EAM, MEAM, ADP]
        RFF[Reactive Force Fields<br/>ReaxFF, COMB]
        ML[Machine Learning Potentials<br/>SNAP, MLIAP]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Components"
        PS[Pair Style Classes]
        NBL[Neighbor Lists]
        FCM[Force Computing Methods]
    end
    
    subgraph "Data Files"
        PF[Potential Files<br/>.tersoff, .meam, .reax]
        CF[Control Files<br/>ReaxFF control]
    end
    
    BP --> PS
    EAM --> PS
    RFF --> PS
    ML --> PS
    
    PS --> NBL
    PS --> FCM
    
    PS --> PF
    RFF --> CF
```

The modular design enables efficient neighbor list management, parallel force computation, and integration with various analysis and output commands. Each potential family inherits from base pair style classes while implementing specialized force and energy calculations.

Sources: [examples/tersoff/in.tersoff](examples/tersoff/in.tersoff#L53-L54), [examples/meam/in.meam](examples/meam/in.meam#L10-L11), [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L8-L9)

## Bond-Order Potentials

Bond-order potentials derive from the Tersoff formalism, which models covalent bonding through bond-order functions that depend on the local coordination environment. These potentials capture the essential physics of covalent materials including silicon, carbon, and compound semiconductors, where bond strength varies with coordination number and local geometry.

The Tersoff potential energy follows the form:

E = ½ Σi Σj≠i f_C(r_ij) [f_R(r_ij) + b_ij f_A(r_ij)]

where f_R and f_A are repulsive and attractive terms, f_C is a cutoff function, and b_ij is the bond-order parameter that depends on the local environment through angle-dependent terms:

b_ij = (1 + βⁿ ζ_ijⁿ)^(-1/2n)

ζ_ij = Σk≠i,j f_C(r_ik) g(θ_ijk) exp[α³(r_ij - r_ik)³]

This formulation automatically reduces bond strength as coordination increases, explaining the behavior of defects, surfaces, and amorphous materials.

Sources: [potentials/Si.tersoff](potentials/Si.tersoff#L1-L20), [examples/tersoff/in.tersoff](examples/tersoff/in.tersoff#L51-L54)

### Tersoff Variants and Implementation

LAMMPS provides multiple Tersoff implementations optimized for different applications and computational platforms:

| Potential Style | Features | Use Cases | Example |
|----------------|----------|-----------|---------|
| **tersoff** | Standard Tersoff | Si, Ge, C, compound semiconductors | [Si.tersoff](potentials/Si.tersoff) |
| **tersoff/mod** | Modified parametrization | Improved accuracy for specific materials | Si.tersoff.mod |
| **tersoff/mod/c** | C-optimized version | Enhanced performance on CPUs | Si.tersoff.modc |
| **tersoff/shift** | Shifted potential | Avoid energy discontinuities at cutoff | BNC.tersoff with shift |

The implementation demonstrates progressive testing from basic to modified variants within the same simulation framework:

```lammps
# Standard Tersoff
pair_style tersoff
pair_coeff * * Si.tersoff Si Si Si Si Si Si Si Si

# Modified Tersoff
pair_style tersoff/mod
pair_coeff * * Si.tersoff.mod Si Si Si Si Si Si Si Si
```

Sources: [examples/tersoff/in.tersoff](examples/tersoff/in.tersoff#L66-L72), [examples/tersoff/in.tersoff](examples/tersoff/in.tersoff#L98-L107)

### AIREBO and Adaptive Intermolecular Potentials

The AIREBO (Adaptive Intermolecular Reactive Empirical Bond Order) potential extends the Tersoff formalism to include non-bonded interactions and torsional terms, enabling simulations of hydrocarbon systems with accurate treatment of both covalent bonding and van der Waals interactions. This makes AIREBO particularly suitable for polymers, graphene, and hydrocarbon phases.

AIREBO combines three components:

E_total = E_REBO + E_LJ + E_torsion

- **E_REBO**: Reactive empirical bond-order terms (similar to Brenner potential)
- **E_LJ**: Lennard-Jones non-bonded interactions with adaptive switching
- **E_torsion**: Dihedral angle terms for hydrocarbon torsion

The potential automatically switches between bonded and non-bonded descriptions based on interatomic distance, enabling simulation of chemical reactions and bond breaking/formation events.

Sources: [potentials/CH.airebo](potentials/CH.airebo#L1-L15)

## Embedded Atom Method (EAM) Potentials

Embedded Atom Method potentials represent the cornerstone of metallic system simulation, modeling metallic bonding through an energy functional formalism where each atom's energy depends on the local electron density contributed by neighboring atoms. This approach naturally captures many-body effects essential for metals, including surface energies, defect formation, and elastic properties.

The EAM energy expression takes the form:

E_total = Σi F_i(ρ_i) + ½ Σi Σj≠i φ_ij(r_ij)

where F_i is the embedding energy as a function of the local electron density ρ_i = Σj≠i f_j(r_ij), and φ_ij is a pairwise potential function. The embedding function F captures many-body effects through its non-linear dependence on the local electron density.

Sources: [potentials/Cu_u3.eam](potentials/Cu_u3.eam#L1-L30), [potentials/README](potentials/README#L10-L15)

### EAM Variants and File Formats

LAMMPS supports multiple EAM implementations optimized for different material classes and computational requirements:

| Variant | File Format | Materials | Key Features |
|---------|-------------|-----------|--------------|
| **eam** | .eam | Pure metals | Simple single-element format |
| **eam/alloy** | .eam.alloy | Binary/multi-component | Multiple species support |
| **eam/fs** | .eam.fs | Alloys, compounds | Finnis-Sinclair formalism |
| **eam/cd** | .eam | Metals + charge transfer | Charge-dependent embedding |

The alloy format enables simulation of complex multi-component systems:

```lammps
# Multi-component EAM/alloy for Cu-Zr alloy
pair_style eam/alloy
pair_coeff * * CuZr_mm.eam.fs Cu Zr
```

Sources: [potentials/CuZr_mm.eam.fs](potentials/CuZr_mm.eam.fs#L1-L20), [potentials/CuNi.eam.alloy](potentials/CuNi.eam.alloy#L1-L20)

### Modified Embedded Atom Method (MEAM)

MEAM extends EAM by including angular-dependent contributions to the electron density, enabling more accurate description of directional bonding in alloys, semiconductors, and metals with covalent character. MEAM computes a background electron density that depends on bond angles through partial electron densities:

ρ_i^(a) = Σj≠i f(r_ij) G_a(θ_ijk)

where a indexes different electron density components (s, p, d) and G_a are angular functions. The total electron density is a non-linear combination of these partial densities:

ρ_i = (ρ_i^(0))^(2/3) + (ρ_i^(1))^(2/3) + (ρ_i^(2))^(2/3) + ... ^(3/2)

MEAM requires two input files: a library file with element-specific parameters and a potential file defining element-element interactions.

Sources: [examples/meam/in.meam](examples/meam/in.meam#L10-L11), [potentials/library.meam](potentials/library.meam#L1-L30)

```lammps
# MEAM for SiC compound
pair_style meam
pair_coeff * * library.meam Si C SiC.meam Si C
```

The MEAM implementation demonstrates the multi-file approach common to complex potentials, separating element parameters (library.meam) from specific interaction parameters (SiC.meam).

Sources: [examples/meam/in.meam](examples/meam/in.meam#L10-L11)

## Reactive Force Fields

Reactive force fields represent the most sophisticated class of potentials in LAMMPS, capable of simulating chemical reactions, bond breaking and formation, and charge transfer with near-quantum mechanical accuracy at a fraction of the computational cost. These potentials employ sophisticated functional forms and self-consistent charge equilibration to capture dynamic changes in chemical bonding.

Sources: [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L1-L10)

### ReaxFF (Reactive Force Field)

ReaxFF provides a comprehensive force field for hydrocarbons and organic molecules, implementing bond-order based energy terms that smoothly transition between bonded and non-bonded interactions. The total ReaxFF energy includes 14 distinct contributions:

E_total = E_bond + E_over + E_under + E_val + E_pen + E_coa + E_tors + E_conj + E_vdWaals + E_Coulomb + E_Hbond + E_4-body + E_field + E_charge

ReaxFF uses distance-dependent bond orders that continuously approach zero and unity, enabling smooth bond breaking and formation:

BO'_ij = exp[ p_be1 * ((r_ij/p_be2)^p_be3 + (r_ij/p_be4)^p_be4) ]

BO_ij = BO'_ij^(1/(1 + exp(p_bf1 * (r_ij - p_bf2))))

> [!TIP]
> ReaxFF requires QEq (Charge Equilibration) fixes for self-consistent charge calculation. The fix qeq/reaxff command must be specified to enable dynamic charge redistribution during simulation, which is critical for modeling polarizable systems and reactions involving charge transfer.

Sources: [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L8-L9), [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L11-L26)

The ReaxFF implementation provides detailed energy decomposition for analysis:

```lammps
pair_style reaxff control.reax_c.rdx
pair_coeff * * ffield.reax C H O N

compute reax all pair reaxff
variable eb equal c_reax[1]  # Bond energy
variable ea equal c_reax[2]  # Over-coordination energy
variable elp equal c_reax[3]  # Under-coordination energy
variable emol equal c_reax[4]  # Valence angle energy
variable ev equal c_reax[5]  # Penalty energy
variable epen equal c_reax[6]  # Coordination angle energy
variable ecoa equal c_reax[7]  # Torsion angle energy
variable ehb equal c_reax[8]  # Conjugation energy
variable et equal c_reax[9]  # Van der Waals energy
variable eco equal c_reax[10]  # Coulomb energy

fix 2 all qeq/reaxff 1 0.0 10.0 1.0e-6 reaxff
```

Sources: [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L11-L26), [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L32-L33)

### COMB (Charge Optimized Many-Body)

COMB potentials extend the EAM/MEAM framework with self-consistent charge equilibration, enabling reactive simulations of metal-oxide systems, semiconductor-oxide interfaces, and complex ceramics. COMB combines EAM/MEAM formalism with variable charge schemes similar to ReaxFF but with different functional forms optimized for inorganic materials.

COMB3 represents the latest generation with improved accuracy and stability for multi-component systems. The potential requires comprehensive parameter files containing element properties, pair parameters, and charge transfer parameters.

Sources: [potentials/ffield.comb3](potentials/ffield.comb3#L1-L30)

## Machine Learning Potentials

Machine learning potentials represent the frontier of interatomic potential development in LAMMPS, combining physically-informed descriptors with machine learning regression to achieve near-DFT accuracy at MD computational cost. These potentials learn energy landscapes from reference quantum mechanical calculations while maintaining computational efficiency through local atomic environment descriptors.

Sources: [examples/snap/README.md](examples/snap/README.md#L1-L20)

### SNAP (Spectral Neighbor Analysis Potential)

SNAP computes bispectrum components of the local atomic environment, providing a complete rotationally invariant descriptor of local atomic structure. The total energy is expressed as a linear combination of bispectrum components:

E_total = Σi [β_0 + Σk Σl Σm β_klm B_klm(i)]

where B_klm(i) are bispectrum components computed from neighbor positions and β_klm are linear coefficients fitted to reference data. The bispectrum components provide a unique fingerprint of local atomic structure that captures bond angles, coordination numbers, and higher-order correlations.

> [!TIP]
> SNAP requires both parameter files (.snapparam) defining descriptor computation and coefficient files (.snapcoeff) containing fitted linear parameters. The two-file structure separates computational parameters (cutoff radius, weighting functions) from physics-specific fitting parameters, enabling reuse of descriptor infrastructure across different materials.

Sources: [examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A](examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A#L27), [potentials/Ta06A.snapparam](potentials/Ta06A.snapparam#L1-L20)

SNAP implementation in LAMMPS demonstrates clean separation of descriptor setup and potential parameters:

```lammps
# SNAP potential for Tantalum
include Ta06A.snap  # Sets pair_style and pair_coeff
```

The included file contains:
```lammps
pair_style snap
pair_coeff * * Ta06A.snapcoeff Ta
```

Sources: [examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A](examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A#L27)

### Quadratic SNAP and MLIAP Framework

Quadratic SNAP extends the linear SNAP model by including pairwise terms, enabling more accurate description of interactions across a wide range of chemical environments. The energy expression becomes:

E = Σi β_0 + Σi Σk β_k B_k(i) + Σi Σj Σk Σl β_kl B_k(i) B_l(j)

The MLIAP (Machine Learning Interatomic Potential) framework provides a unified interface for machine learning potentials, supporting multiple descriptor types (SNAP, ACE, neural networks) and various regression methods. This architecture enables rapid experimentation with different ML potential formulations.

Sources: [potentials/Cu_Zuo_JPCA2020.quadratic.snapcoeff](potentials/Cu_Zuo_JPCA2020.quadratic.snapcoeff#L1-L20), [examples/snap/in.snap.compute.quadratic](examples/snap/in.snap.compute.quadratic#L1-L30)

## Comparison of Potential Families

Selecting the appropriate many-body or reactive potential requires understanding trade-offs between accuracy, computational efficiency, and applicability to specific materials and phenomena.

| Potential Family | Accuracy | Computational Cost | Applicable Materials | Key Strengths |
|------------------|----------|-------------------|---------------------|---------------|
| **Tersoff/AIREBO** | High for covalent systems | Medium | Si, C, semiconductors, hydrocarbons | Defects, surfaces, amorphous phases |
| **EAM/MEAM** | High for metals | Low-Medium | Pure metals, alloys, intermetallics | Elastic properties, grain boundaries |
| **ReaxFF** | Near-DFT for reactions | High | Organic molecules, metal oxides, energetic materials | Chemical reactions, bond breaking |
| **COMB** | High for ceramics | Medium-High | Oxides, carbides, interfaces | Metal-oxide systems |
| **SNAP/MLIAP** | Near-DFT for fitted systems | Medium | Broad (depends on training data) | High accuracy across diverse environments |
| **ILP (Interlayer Potential)** | High for layered materials | Medium | Graphene, MoS2, h-BN | Intercalation, tribology |

Sources: [potentials/SiC.tersoff](potentials/SiC.tersoff#L1-L10), [potentials/FeCH_BOP_I.poly](potentials/FeCH_BOP_I.poly#L1-L10)

## Advanced Features and Optimizations

Many-body potentials in LAMMPS support advanced computational techniques for handling large-scale simulations and complex material systems.

### Neighbor List Management

Reactive potentials with short-ranged interactions and bond-order calculations require careful neighbor list configuration to balance accuracy and efficiency:

```lammps
neighbor 2.5 bin
neigh_modify every 10 delay 0 check no
```

The `check no` option is particularly important for reactive potentials where bond formation can create new interactions within the cutoff during a timestep.

Sources: [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L28-L29)

### Hybrid Potential Schemes

LAMMPS enables combining multiple potentials through hybrid pair styles, allowing different interaction types to be modeled with appropriate potentials:

```lammps
# Combine SNAP for metal-metal interactions with pair potential for metal-gas
pair_style hybrid/overlay snap table
pair_coeff * * W_2940_2017_2_He_JW2013.snapcoeff W
pair_coeff * 2 W_He_JW2013.table He
```

This capability is essential for modeling interfaces, surfaces, and multi-component systems where different physics govern different interaction types.

Sources: [examples/snap/in.snap.hybrid.WSNAP.HePair](examples/snap/in.snap.hybrid.WSNAP.HePair#L1-L20)

### Grid and Parallel Implementation

Machine learning potentials support efficient grid-based computation and parallel scaling through optimized descriptor calculations. The SNAP implementation demonstrates advanced parallelization strategies:

```lammps
# Grid-based SNAP for large systems
pair_style snap 0.8 1.0
pair_coeff * * W_2940_2017_2.snapcoeff W
```

The parameters (0.8 cutoff, 1.0 processing radius) control the trade-off between accuracy and computational cost.

Sources: [examples/snap/in.snap.grid](examples/snap/in.snap.grid#L1-L30), [examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A](examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A#L36-L38)

## Practical Implementation Guide

Implementing many-body and reactive potentials in LAMMPS requires attention to input script structure, file organization, and computational parameters.

### Essential Setup Steps

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Select Potential Type] --> B[Choose Variant]
    B --> C[Obtain Parameter Files]
    C --> D[Configure Units]
    D --> E[Define Pair Style]
    E --> F[Set Pair Coefficients]
    F --> G[Configure Neighbor List]
    G --> H[Add Special Fixes]
    H --> I[Run and Validate]
    
    %% 将具体变体的选择路径指向 C (Obtain Parameter Files)
    B --> |Tersoff| B1["tersoff/mod/shift"]
    B1 --> C
    
    B --> |EAM| B2["eam/alloy/fs"]
    B2 --> C
    
    B --> |ReaxFF| B3["reaxff + qeq"]
    B3 --> C
    
    B --> |SNAP| B4["snap + coeff files"]
    B4 --> C
    
    %% 将具体的 Fix 设置路径指向 I (Run and Validate)
    %% 假设这些是 H 节点下的具体设置，完成后运行
    H --> |ReaxFF| H1["fix qeq/reaxff"]
    H1 --> I
    
    H --> |MEAM| H2["library + meam files"]
    H2 --> I
    
    H --> |COMB| H3["comb3 parameters"]
    H3 --> I
```

Sources: [examples/tersoff/in.tersoff](examples/tersoff/in.tersoff#L5-L9), [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L3-L6)

### File Organization Best Practices

LAMMPS potential files follow standardized conventions with metadata headers:

```
# DATE: 2021-02-09
# UNITS: metal
# CONTRIBUTOR: Jane Doe (janedoe@university.edu)
# CITATION: J. Smith et al., Phys. Rev. B 123, 456 (2021)
# ... parameter data ...
```

The UNITS field enables automatic validation that potential parameters match simulation units, preventing unit conversion errors.

Sources: [potentials/README](potentials/README#L40-L60)

### Performance Optimization Strategies

Many-body potential performance depends heavily on neighbor list configuration and computational hardware:

| Optimization | Effect | Applicable Potentials |
|-------------|--------|----------------------|
| **Increased neighbor skin** | Fewer list rebuilds | All potentials |
| **Reduced neighbor checks** | Faster neighbor list building | Reactive potentials |
| **GPU acceleration** | 3-10x speedup | SNAP, ReaxFF variants |
| **Kokkos portability** | Multi-platform optimization | SNAP, MLIAP |
| **Neighbor stencil optimization** | Efficient neighbor search | Tersoff, EAM |

> [!TIP]
> For reactive potentials like ReaxFF with bond breaking/formation, use larger neighbor skin (0.8-1.0× cutoff) with reduced rebuild frequency, but disable neighbor checking (`check no`) to prevent spurious force discontinuities when new bonds form within the cutoff.

Sources: [examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx](examples/reaxff/in.reaxff.rdx#L28-L29), [examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A](examples/snap/in.snap.Ta06A#L37-L38)

## Potential Selection and Validation

Choosing the appropriate many-body or reactive potential requires systematic evaluation of material properties and simulation requirements.

### Validation Workflow

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Define Target Materials & Properties] --> B[Search Available Potentials]
    B --> C[Review Literature & Citations]
    C --> D[Run Test Simulations]
    D --> E[Compare with Reference Data]
    E --> F{Accuracy Sufficient?}
    F -->|Yes| G[Proceed with Production]
    F -->|No| H[Explore Alternative Potentials]
    H --> B
```

Critical validation properties include lattice constants, elastic constants, defect formation energies, surface energies, and, for reactive potentials, reaction barriers and product energies.

Sources: [potentials/README](potentials/README#L20-L35)

### Reference Databases and Community Resources

LAMMPS potential files serve as demonstrations and starting points rather than validated implementations. For production simulations, consult authoritative databases:

- **NIST Interatomic Potentials Repository**: Verified potentials with citation tracking
- **KIM (Knowledgebase of Interatomic Models)**: Standardized potential library with automatic property testing
- **IPR (Interatomic Potentials Repository)**: Community-curated potential collection

Always verify potential accuracy by comparing LAMMPS results with published reference data for the specific properties and conditions relevant to your application.

Sources: [potentials/README](potentials/README#L20-L35)

### Advanced Applications

Many-body and reactive potentials enable sophisticated simulations across multiple domains:

- **Materials discovery**: High-throughput screening of alloy compositions using EAM/MEAM
- **Catalysis**: Surface reactions and adsorption processes using ReaxFF or COMB
- **Nanomaterials**: Graphene, nanotubes, and 2D materials using AIREBO or ILP
- **Defect engineering**: Vacancy migration, dislocation dynamics using SNAP-trained potentials
- **Radiation damage**: Cascades in metals using high-fidelity ML potentials
- **Polymer chemistry**: Cross-linking, degradation using AIREBO or ReaxFF

These applications leverage the unique capabilities of reactive potentials to capture bond rearrangement and many-body effects to describe complex material behavior.

Sources: [potentials/MoS.rebomos](potentials/MoS.rebomos#L1-L10), [potentials/Cu_Zuo_JPCA2020.snapcoeff](potentials/Cu_Zuo_JPCA2020.snapcoeff#L1-L20)
